- [statement] A small 2024 survey combining autonomic-dysfunction and PD respondents reported high satisfaction with telehealth, but limited internet connectivity and impaired fine motor movements hindered access. Its mixed 25-person sample does not establish PD-wide satisfaction rates. (low confidence) — https://telehealthandmedicinetoday.com/index.php/journal/article/view/461/1075 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Recent reviews state that no disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson's disease has been established: one says there are currently no disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), and a trial-pipeline analysis says there are still no treatments to modify the course of the disease. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-17) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01483-9
- [statement] A meta-analysis of therapeutic massage for motor symptoms in PD (Kang et al.; 363 participants in seven RCTs and one randomized pilot-control study) reported greater total effectiveness than control (RR: 1.33, 95% CI 1.14–1.55) and better UPDRS-III scores (SMD = −0.46, 95% CI −0.67, −0.24) but no better daily-living outcomes (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI −0.40, 0.10, p = 0.23), and a separate systematic review of 12 studies (Angelopoulou et al.) concluded that, despite methodological concerns, there is a wide range of safe massage techniques with beneficial effects on both motor and non-motor symptoms of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Two systematic reviews found no significant advantage of acupuncture over placebo acupuncture on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS): the Lee et al. review in Movement Disorders (eleven RCTs) pooled three placebo-controlled RCTs (n = 96, WMD, 5.7; 95% CI -2.8 to 14.2, P = 0.19) and judged the evidence 'not convincing', and the Noh et al. meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) reported that its results failed to show acupuncture significantly more effective than placebo acupuncture in total UPDRS. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18618661/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] In Yan et al., a single-center double-blind RCT in China that randomized people with PD and sleep complaints to real or sham acupuncture for 4 weeks (83 enrolled, 78 analyzed), Parkinson Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores rose more with real than sham acupuncture after 4 weeks of treatment (19.75; 95% CI 11.02-28.49; P <.001), while the authors report that no statistically significant improvements in motor symptoms and daytime sleepiness were observed among the secondary outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Evidence-quality statements on massage in PD are cautious: Kang et al. report approximately 42.9% low risk, 42.9% some concerns and 14.3% high risk of overall bias and note that complete blinding of participants and personnel was impossible; Angelopoulou et al. cite methodological concerns, say longitudinal studies are needed, and report that Yin Tui Na technique combined with acupuncture was associated with worse motor scores; and Parkinson's UK says research suggests massage may help to reduce pain, anxiety and depression, although there is no conclusive evidence. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommendation 1.7.4 reads 'Consider the Alexander Technique for people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing balance or motor function problems', and Parkinson's UK states that NICE clinical guidelines recommend that people with Parkinson's consider the Alexander technique to help with balance or motor problems (a page whose footer says 'Last updated November 2018'). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Parkinson's UK states that there is little scientific evidence that complementary therapies can slow, stop or reverse the development of Parkinson's and that it does not endorse any particular therapies, while the Parkinson's Foundation says some therapies have even shown promise in Parkinson's studies but research is still in the initial stages and that acupuncture is also sometimes used to alleviate PD pain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Meta-analyses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report better UPDRS results than the comparison arm while describing the evidence as limited: one meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) found that combined acupuncture and conventional medication showed significant improvements in total UPDRS, UPDRS I, UPDRS II and UPDRS III compared with conventional medication alone and rated the methodological quality of the RCTs low, and Yu et al. (50 RCTs, n = 3,248; acupuncture modalities combined with standard PD therapy) report acupuncture significantly outperforming Western medicine across all UPDRS domains while stating that the overall certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to low across most outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] In a three-group RCT in ninety-three people with idiopathic PD (24 lessons in the Alexander Technique, 24 sessions of massage, or no additional intervention), the Alexander Technique group improved compared with the no additional intervention group on the Self-assessment Parkinson's Disease Disability Scale at best (p = 0.04) and at worst (p = 0.01), with the comparative improvement maintained at six-month follow-up; a systematic review of Alexander Technique lessons (Woodman and Moore) concluded there was moderate evidence in Parkinson's-associated disability, and Parkinson's UK describes the evidence as one study of fewer than 100 people. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12428818/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Sources differ on electroacupuncture added to anti-parkinsonian drug therapy: the Cho et al. guideline reports that in three RCTs electroacupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drugs, compared with drug therapy alone, showed no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness and grades it 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low), whereas Yu et al., in an analysis of 50 RCTs (n = 3,248), report that among all modalities electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Sham-controlled RCTs of acupuncture for PD-related fatigue found no significant difference between real and sham acupuncture: Kluger et al. (ninety-four PD patients, 6 weeks of biweekly treatment) reported significant improvements in both groups at 6 and 12 weeks without significant between-group differences, and Kong et al. (forty PD patients, 5 weeks) reported the same pattern; the Cui et al. review found fatigue showed no difference from sham (SMD 0.10) and graded certainty for fatigue very low. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Authors differ on what sham-controlled acupuncture results imply: Kluger et al. conclude that PD-related fatigue joins the conditions that acupuncture helps primarily through nonspecific or placebo effects, and Kong et al. judge real and sham acupuncture equally effective for PD-related fatigue and likely due to nonspecific or placebo effects, whereas Kwon et al. report that sham acupuncture combined with conventional medicine was superior to conventional medicine alone in their network meta-analysis and suggest that a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] No serious adverse events were reported in the acupuncture trials and reviews read, although mild-event reporting was inconsistent: an earlier meta-analysis, Kluger et al. and Cui et al. each report no serious adverse events; Yan et al. report no severe adverse events in either group, with the most common self-reported acupuncture-related events being severe tremor; bleeding, numbness, or infection; and sharp pain during treatment; Cui et al. note that reporting of mild adverse events was variable and often not described in detail; and Parkinson's UK lists slight pain, bleeding or bruising, and feeling sick, drowsy or faint as minor, short-lived side effects. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Appraisals of the acupuncture-for-PD literature rate its quality low: an overview of 11 systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Huang et al.) rated all included reviews very-low-quality on AMSTAR-2, with GRADE revealing 20 studies with very-low-quality evidence, 9 with low-quality evidence, 3 with moderate-quality evidence, and 0 with high-quality evidence, and its authors say their conclusion must be interpreted cautiously; the York CRD abstract of the Lee et al. review reports that seven RCTs were of low quality, and Noh et al. rated the methodological quality of their included RCTs low. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482669/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] The complementary-medicine clinical practice guideline for idiopathic PD (Cho et al.) grades concomitant use of acupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drug therapy as 'should be considered' (strength of recommendation B, level of evidence low; twenty-one RCTs) and moxibustion as 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
- [statement] Positive findings on cannabis in PD come from open-label or uncontrolled designs that the sources treat with caution: a 2026 single-center open-label prospective cohort of 68 patients initiating medical cannabis reported improvements in the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale total score at 3 months, with a dropout rate of 26.5%, and its authors call the findings exploratory; an earlier systematic review states that positive effects described in uncontrolled studies have not been confirmed by the few and small RCTs; and the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement says studies suggesting non-motor benefit are generally small, uncontrolled and open label, and that more rigorous research is needed. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42304702/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] In the CBD-PD-BRH trial (Parkinsonism & Related Disorders, volume 135, June 2025), sixty PD patients were randomized to sublingual CBD or placebo and 51 were analysed; the authors report that the primary outcome, MoCA delayed recall, showed no group differences, that the CBD group improved naming scores (mean difference 0.37, 95 % CI 0.01 to 0.73) at a mean CBD dose of 26 mg/day, and that alkaline phosphatase was elevated in the CBD group with no serious side effects in either group. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1353802025005826 · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] In an exploratory double-blind trial of 21 PD patients without dementia or comorbid psychiatric conditions (placebo, CBD 75 mg/day or CBD 300 mg/day; seven per group), Chagas et al. found no statistically significant differences in UPDRS scores, plasma BDNF levels or H(1)-MRS measures, while mean total PDQ-39 scores differed between the placebo and CBD 300 mg/day groups (p = 0.05); the authors write that their findings point to a possible effect of CBD in improving quality of life measures and that studies with larger samples and specific objectives are required before definitive conclusions can be drawn. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25237116/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] In the Colorado phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral CBD/THC in PD (61 randomized: 31 CBD/THC, 30 placebo; final dose of 2.5mg/kg/day), motor MDS-UPDRS was reduced by 4.57 with CBD/THC and 2.77 with placebo and the between-group difference was not significant (-1.80, p = 0.379); the registry record NCT03582137, which gives the same enrollment window (9/5/2018 to 1/4/2022) and the same 61 randomized, posts a net mean difference of -1.8049 and p = 0.3785; the authors report that sleep, cognition and activities of daily living showed a treatment effect favoring placebo, and conclude that the brief duration and strong placebo response limit interpretation but there was no benefit, perhaps worsened cognition and sleep, and many mild adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11102313/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] As published, the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement (May 2020) says that, given the lack of any clear data supporting the use of cannabis in PD, the Foundation does not endorse its use for PD symptoms or to modify disease progression; the Foundation's web page states that there is no conclusive evidence marijuana helps with PD symptoms; and a document hosted on the Michael J. Fox Foundation website, with content current to March 2022, states that controlled trials have not yet proven the safety or benefit of cannabis in Parkinson's. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] The 2014 American Academy of Neurology systematic review of medical marijuana in selected neurologic disorders concluded that oral cannabis extract is probably ineffective for treating levodopa-induced dyskinesias in patients with Parkinson disease; the PubMed record title of this report carries the label [RETIRED], and the Parkinson's Foundation 2020 statement cites the same AAN conclusion. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24778283/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported for cannabinoids versus placebo in PD include: the Fernandes et al. meta-analysis of seven randomized trials reports increased risk of confusion (risk ratio, 4.44; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-16.87) and dizziness (risk ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.65-4.68); the Colorado CBD/THC trial reports twice as many treatment emergent adverse events in the CBD/THC group, most of them mild; and the São Paulo cannabis-oil trial reports irritability more frequent in the CBD/THC group (P = 0.005). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] Randomized trials report different results for non-motor symptoms in PD: Peball et al. (phase II enriched-enrollment randomized withdrawal trial of nabilone; 47 patients began open-label titration and 19 patients received nabilone or placebo) reported a MDS-UPDRS-I difference of 1.63 (95% CI 0.09 to 3.18, p = 0.030) at week 4 and interpret this as potential efficacy of nabilone, with one author an employee of the study-drug manufacturer; Kubota et al. (CBD/THC oil versus placebo) reported no significant differences in other non-motor scales; and the Messak et al. meta-analysis found non-motor symptoms not significantly improved (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32757413/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis or cannabinoids in PD, published between 2022 and 2026, conclude that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit: Urbi et al. report that no compelling evidence was found to recommend the use of cannabis in PD patients, while also identifying a potential benefit with respect to alleviation of PD related tremor, anxiety, pain, improvement of sleep quality and quality of life; Messak et al. report that cannabinoids have not shown significant benefit in PD; Fernandes et al. report that current randomized evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful benefits. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34958046/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] In the Messak et al. meta-analysis of randomized trials of cannabinoids in PD (eleven RCTs identified, six eligible for meta-analysis), cannabinoids did not significantly improve PD severity (SMD = 0.16, p = 0.27), motor examination (SMD=-0.08, p = 0.57) or non-motor symptoms (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94); the authors state that the nabilone benefit signal for non-motor symptoms represents a distinct question warranting dedicated trials. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] Two small randomized crossover trials of cannabinoids for levodopa-induced dyskinesia in PD reported opposite results: Sieradzan et al. (Neurology, 2001; n = 7) reported that nabilone significantly reduced levodopa-induced dyskinesia, whereas Carroll et al. (Neurology, 2004; 19 randomized, seventeen completed) reported no evidence of a treatment effect of oral cannabis extract on levodopa-induced dyskinesia; a systematic review of RCTs in movement disorders states that of three PD RCTs with levodopa-induced dyskinesia as primary outcome, only one, using nabilone, showed a reduction. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11739835/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson's Foundation exercise page lists biking, running, Tai Chi, yoga, Pilates, dance, weight training, non-contact boxing and qi gong among exercise types that all have positive effects on PD symptoms; the APTA guideline says results across community-based exercise modes appear comparable for impairment and participation-based measures, suggesting no 1 mode is superior to another, while other comparisons favor 1 intervention over another and the essential components that distinguish more from less effective programs are not clear; a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) concludes that superiority over other exercise modalities remains uncertain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise
- [statement] In the Duncan and Earhart randomized trial, 62 participants were assigned to a twice-weekly community-based Argentine tango program or a no-intervention control group and assessed off anti-Parkinson medication; on the primary MDS-UPDRS-3 outcome the control group showed no significant change over 12 months whereas the tango group had a reduction of 28.7% (12.8 points), and the authors suggest that long-term participation in tango may modify progression of disability in PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21959675/
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline for physical therapist management of Parkinson disease states that physical therapists should recommend community-based exercise to reduce motor disease severity and improve nonmotor symptoms, functional outcomes, and quality of life, rating evidence strength as high and recommendation strength as strong. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] In the Li et al. randomized trial (NCT00611481), 195 patients with Hoehn and Yahr stage 1 to 4 Parkinson's disease were assigned to tai chi, resistance training or stretching for 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks, and the tai chi group performed better than the resistance-training and stretching groups on the primary outcome of maximum excursion (between-group differences of 5.55 and 11.98 percentage points) and on directional control (10.45 and 11.38 percentage points). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3285459/
- [statement] Meta-analytic findings on tai chi and qigong and quality of life in Parkinson's disease differ: Song et al. (15 RCTs) reported improved quality of life (ES=-0.393, p<.001), whereas a meta-analysis of seven systematic reviews (Fidan et al.) and a meta-analysis of thirteen RCTs of traditional Chinese exercises (Song et al., later version) reported no statistically significant quality-of-life effect. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of boxing for Parkinson's disease differ: Wang et al. (13 studies, 402 patients, pre-post assessments of boxing interventions) conclude that boxing exercise can effectively improve both motor and non-motor symptoms with safety and high adherence, whereas Gonzalez-Devesa et al. (13 studies) report no significant pooled effect on functional mobility, balance, motor symptoms, gait and cardiorespiratory fitness and call the evidence uncertain, and Hernandez-Martinez et al. (eight studies, 100 older people) conclude that boxing does not significantly improve balance, cardiorespiratory fitness and health-related quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11983467/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of yoga in Parkinson's disease report benefit with caveats about robustness: Ban et al. (ten studies, 359 participants) report better motor status (MD = −5.64) with yoga and state that their results should be interpreted with caution, Suárez-Iglesias et al. report that a meta-analysis on five RCTs found yoga more effective than passive control for motor symptoms, whereas a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) found that the significant effects of yoga did not prove robust in sensitivity analysis. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8275425/
- [statement] A meta-analysis of tai chi and qigong trials (Song et al.; 15 RCTs, 755 subjects) reported improvement in UPDRS III (ES=-0.444) and balance (ES=0.544), rated methodological bias low in 6 studies, moderate in 7 and high in 2, and noted that funnel plots suggested some degree of publication bias; a later meta-analysis of traditional Chinese exercises (thirteen RCTs, 859 patients) reported UPDRS-III MD -4.30 and Berg Balance Scale MD 2.63 versus usual control and noted that only one included study used a double-blind procedure. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/
- [statement] On dance and motor symptom severity the sources differ: the European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a weak recommendation against using dance to improve movement functions (UPDRS III), whereas two meta-analyses of randomized trials (Ismail et al., 20 RCTs; Carapellotti et al., sixteen RCTs) report better MDS-UPDRS scores with dance than in non-dancers or no-intervention controls. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf
- [statement] The European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a strong recommendation for using tai chi to improve movement functions (UPDRS III) and weak recommendations for using it to improve number of falls, balance capacity (BBS), walking speed, stride length, walking distance, functional mobility (TUG), muscle strength and functional reach, based on three CCTs in which 200 pwp participated. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf
- [statement] In a systematic review of sixteen RCTs involving 636 participants with mild to moderate PD, Carapellotti et al. reported that dance was favored over no intervention on MDS-UPDRS III (-2.31 points, p = 0.0004; four studies, n = 160) and balance (0.50 points, p = 0.0007; five studies, n = 206) but not on forward gait velocity (p = 0.44) or PDQ-39 (p = 0.65); an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews (Pinto et al.) reported that dance added to usual care was better than usual care alone for motor symptoms severity, depressive symptoms, balance and functional mobility but not for gait distance and quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] Two randomized trials compared boxing with another active program: in Combs et al. (n = 31; 24-36 sessions of 90 minutes over 12 weeks) the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group while only the boxing group showed significant improvements in gait velocity and endurance, and in Sangarapillai et al. (40 participants, 20-week trial) the sensory exercise group improved in comparison to the boxing group on a group-by-time interaction for the UPDRS-III (P =.036). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23422464/
- [statement] SPARX3 (NCT04284436) is a phase 3 multicenter randomized evaluator-blinded treadmill endurance-exercise trial in persons with PD diagnosed within 3 years and untreated with symptomatic therapy, comparing moderate intensity (60–65% of maximum heart rate) with high intensity (80–85%) at 4 days per week and 30 minutes per session, with change in the MDS-UPDRS motor score (Part III) over 12 months as the primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] For balance training the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality high and recommendation strength strong; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that gait/balance/functional training probably has a moderate beneficial effect on the severity of motor signs (MD -7.50, 95% CI -11.39 to -3.48; moderate confidence; negative estimates reflect improvement); and a physiotherapy meta-analysis of 191 trials reports that balance and gait training, among other modalities, improved motor symptoms, balance, and gait. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] For flexibility exercises the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality low and recommendation strength weak, noting that the evidence quality was rated low because there was only 1 study of moderate quality that met the inclusion criteria; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of flexibility training on the severity of motor signs (MD 4.20, 95% CI -1.61 to 9.92; very low confidence). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] In the PD REHAB multicenter, open-label randomized trial in the United Kingdom (762 patients with mild to moderate PD; 381 randomized to physiotherapy and occupational therapy and 381 to no therapy), there was no difference between groups at 3 months in the primary outcome, the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living score (difference 0.5 points; 95% CI -0.7 to 1.7), and the authors concluded that the evidence does not support the use of low-dose, patient-centered, goal-directed physiotherapy and occupational therapy in patients in the early stages of PD; the NIHR Health Technology Assessment report of the same trial concluded that NHS physiotherapy and occupational therapy did not produce immediate or long-term clinically meaningful improvements in ADL or quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD, Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] The Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs (7837 participants, mostly mild to moderate disease) found little evidence of differences between exercise types and noted that the exact exercise type might be secondary; the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review reported no evidence that the treatment effect differed across physiotherapy interventions (based on indirect comparisons), and the APTA guideline states that its aerobic exercise studies suggest no single form of aerobic exercise was superior to another. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Adverse-event statements in the sources include the following: the Cochrane network meta-analysis states that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of physical exercise on the risk of adverse events (very low confidence), with falls (18 studies) and pain (10 studies) the most frequently reported events; the APTA guideline reports minor musculoskeletal injuries in some aerobic exercise studies, most of which resolved without incident; the SPARX phase 2 trial reported that anticipated adverse musculoskeletal events were not severe; and PD REHAB reported no difference in adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Reviews report improved motor-severity scores for exercise or physiotherapy versus control: the Cochrane physiotherapy review (39 trials, 1827 participants) reported a UPDRS motor difference of -5.01 points (95% CI -6.30 to -3.72); the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported mean differences of -5.76 for endurance training and -4.96 for strength/resistance training, both rated low confidence, with a stated minimum clinically important difference of -2.5; and a meta-analysis of 18 aerobic-exercise trials (901 patients) reported a standardised mean difference of -0.57 for motor actions. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Sources differ on whether exercise or physiotherapy improved quality of life: the APTA guideline, the Cochrane network meta-analysis (low confidence for gait/balance/functional training) and a large physiotherapy meta-analysis report quality-of-life improvements for some interventions, whereas the PD REHAB trial, the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review and a meta-analysis of aerobic exercise report no significant quality-of-life difference. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Reviews state that follow-up evidence is limited: the Cochrane physiotherapy review found benefit in most outcomes over the short term (less than 3 months), the aerobic exercise meta-analysis reported no valid evidence on follow-up effects, the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis on long-term effects, and the Cochrane network meta-analysis analysed effects only up to six weeks after the intervention; the APTA guideline states that gains appear to dissipate if exercise is discontinued. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] In PD COMM, a pragmatic, UK-based, unblinded, three-arm randomised trial of 388 people with Parkinson's disease and dysarthria, the primary outcome (self-reported Voice Handicap Index total score at three months, where a low score is positive) was lower with LSVT LOUD than with no speech and language therapy (-8.0 points; 99% confidence interval -13.3 to -2.6; P<0.001) and lower than with NHS speech and language therapy (-9.6 points; -14.9 to -4.4). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] In PD COMM, the Voice Handicap Index total score remained lower with LSVT LOUD than with no speech and language therapy at six months (-7.2; 99% confidence interval -13.3 to -1.1) and at 12 months (-6.7; -12.6 to -0.8); the authors write that re-intervention might still be required should the treatment effect wear off or as Parkinson's disease progresses. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71, published 19 July 2017 and last reviewed 19 December 2024, recommends offering speech and language therapy to people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing problems with communication, swallowing or saliva (recommendation 1.7.8), including strategies to improve speech and communication 'such as attention to effort therapies'; Parkinson's UK's summary of the NICE guideline and the Canadian guideline for Parkinson disease (which grades the recommendation A and cites NICE as its source) restate it. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] In a systematic review and meta-analysis of LSVT-BIG (searched to September 2017; three randomised trials of 84 participants with mild Parkinson's disease), UPDRS part III improved more than with physiotherapy exercises or a shorter training protocol (mean difference -3.20; 95% CI -5.18 to -1.23), whereas Timed Up and Go (-0.47; 95% CI -0.99 to 0.06) and 10-metre walk (-0.53; 95% CI -1.07 to 0.01) showed only trends, and the authors call this preliminary, moderate quality evidence; a separate gait-exercise meta-analysis (Ni and colleagues) described the LSVT program as yielding only a trend toward increased walking speed. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28980476/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] Two Cochrane reviews with literature searches up to April 2011 each concluded that evidence was insufficient: the review of speech and language therapy versus placebo or no intervention (three randomised trials, 63 participants) found insufficient evidence to conclusively support or refute efficacy for speech problems in Parkinson's disease, and the review comparing therapy techniques (six trials, 159 patients) found insufficient evidence to support or refute any form of therapy over another; the PD COMM authors summarise the earlier review as showing insufficient evidence because of few trials, limited sample sizes and high risk of bias. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7098084/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] In the Berlin LSVT BIG study (60 patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease randomly assigned to one-to-one LSVT BIG, group Nordic Walking or unsupervised domestic exercises; UPDRS scores from blinded video rating), the mean UPDRS motor improvement at 16 weeks was -5.05 (SD 3.91) with LSVT BIG versus a mild deterioration of 0.58 (SD 3.17) with Nordic Walking and 1.68 (SD 5.95) with domestic exercise, with no significant group differences in quality of life (PDQ39). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20669294/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] In PD COMM, where only adverse events specific to speech and language therapy or serious events related to vocal strain or injury were reported, 93 adverse events (predominately vocal strain) were recorded in the LSVT LOUD group and 46 in the NHS speech and language therapy group, none in the no-therapy group, and no serious adverse events; the authors describe the higher rate of vocal strain with LSVT LOUD as mostly a minor, transient issue. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] Five systematic reviews with meta-analysis of rhythmic auditory cueing, rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) or music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease (Ghai, Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li) each report a positive pooled effect on gait velocity or speed and on stride or step length. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764963/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] The Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li meta-analyses each report no statistically significant pooled effect of RAS or music-based interventions on cadence in Parkinson's disease. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] Meta-analyses of RAS and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease differ on balance and timed up-and-go (TUG) mobility: Wang and colleagues and Lee and Ko report statistically significant pooled improvements (Berg Balance Scale and TUG for Wang and colleagues; TUG for Lee and Ko), whereas Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either, and Li and colleagues report a pooled balance effect that became nonsignificant after sensitivity analysis. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait for music-based therapy and RAS in Parkinson's disease: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects for UPDRS-motor score or Freezing of Gait, whereas Ye and colleagues (18 studies) report significant pooled improvements in UPDRS-III and in the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22166406/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on non-motor outcomes of music-based or arts-based interventions in Parkinson's disease: Lee and Ko report no significant pooled effect on quality of life (SMD = −0.68, p = 0.18), and Liu and colleagues' meta-analysis of 22 studies (928 participants) reports non-significant effects on quality of life, cognition and depressive symptoms, whereas a music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies including 3635 patients (searched from inception to 31 August 2026) reports significant improvements in depression, anxiety and life quality. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] A systematic review of randomized controlled trials of music-based interventions for cognitive rehabilitation in Parkinson's disease, which analyzed three articles, concluded that the results showed no evidence of efficacy for cognitive outcomes, and a randomized trial of a group-based music intervention that enrolled forty-six patients (Pohl and colleagues) states that it does not support efficacy for immediate or lasting gains in dual-tasking, cognition, balance, or freezing of gait. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10415237/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] Trinchillo and colleagues' review states that Butala and colleagues found significant improvements in motor functions after 24 weeks in a randomized crossover trial of weekly group singing, whereas Butala and colleagues' own Parkinsonics trial report states a significant overall-cohort MDS-UPDRS Part III improvement at 24 weeks (Δ = 5.9 points) that became nonsignificant when the baseline was adjusted in mixed linear model analyses, and that they cannot conclusively attribute motor improvements to the singing intervention. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13731696/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] In the ParkinSong controlled trial of 75 people living with Parkinson's disease, which compared a singing-based intervention with an active control condition at 2 dosage levels (weekly vs monthly) over 3 months, intervention participants showed significant improvements in vocal intensity, maximum expiratory pressure and voice-related quality of life compared with controls, with no statistical differences between groups on maximum phonation length or maximum inspiratory pressure at 3 months; a systematic review describes this trial as a non-randomised controlled trial. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31081485/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] In the 'art therapy' meta-analysis by Liu and colleagues of 26 randomized controlled trials (2,756 individuals), the included interventions were 5 music, 14 dance, 2 yoga, 1 mindfulness, 1 theater, 1 virtual-reality game-based, 1 Tai Chi plus yoga and 1 Qigong plus dance studies, and the authors conclude that dance therapy exhibited the most pronounced effects across motor function outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12444631/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] In the OTiP multicentre, assessor-masked randomised controlled trial, 191 patients with Parkinson's disease and self-reported difficulties in daily activities were randomly assigned to 10 weeks of home-based occupational therapy (n=124) or usual care with no occupational therapy (n=67); the adjusted mean difference in Canadian Occupational Performance Measure score at 3 months was in favour of the intervention group (1·2; 95% CI 0·8-1·6; p<0·0001), and there were no adverse events associated with the study. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24726066/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] A Cochrane review of occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease, with electronic searches up to April 2007, identified two trials with 84 patients in total, and its authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the efficacy of occupational therapy in Parkinson's disease; the PD REHAB report describes Cochrane reviews of physiotherapy and occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease as having found insufficient evidence of effectiveness. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6991932/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Three systematic reviews of occupational therapy-related interventions in Parkinson's disease report beneficial findings, with their authors also noting limits on the evidence base: the first (10 studies; 1343 people with Parkinson's disease and 180 caregivers) reported that interventions focussing on meaningful activities were shown to improve perceived occupational performance, and noted that few studies have identified the effectiveness of occupational therapy intervention alone; Tofani et al. (15 randomized controlled trials, 4 in the meta-analysis) reported a significant quality-of-life improvement at 2 to 3 months follow-up (mean difference of −2.08; 95% confidence interval, −2.52 to −1.64) and considered the strength of the evidence moderate because of the limited number of studies; Foster et al. (twenty-two studies) reported strong strength of evidence for physical activity levels and handwriting, moderate for IADL participation and medication adherence, and low for cognitive rehabilitation, and noted that the review is limited by the small number of studies that specifically addressed IADL function. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31599467/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Three sources include cueing among their gait recommendations: the APTA clinical practice guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce motor disease severity and freezing of gait (FOG) and to improve gait outcomes in individuals with Parkinson disease (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong), with aggregate evidence of thirteen high-quality and 16 moderate-quality studies; Keus et al. extracted cueing strategies to improve gait as one of four treatment recommendations based on evidence from more than two controlled trials; and a 2020 systematic review of physical therapy for FOG and gait impairments reports that cueing strategies (visual and auditory) reduce FOG with a good category A recommendation. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Three systematic reviews or meta-analyses report improved gait speed or velocity with auditory cueing in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis of cueing studies (searches up to September 2011) reported significant improvement of velocity with auditory cueing (Hedge g=.544; 95% CI,.294-.795); Ghai et al. (50 studies, 1892 participants) reported an overall positive effect on gait velocity, stride length, and a negative effect on cadence with application of auditory cueing; and Nascimento et al. (2024; ten trials involving 309 participants) reported that walking training with auditory cueing improved walking speed by 0.09 m/s (95% CI 0.02 to 0.15) more than walking training alone, which the authors describe as low-quality evidence. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23127307/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Sources differ on which type of external cue performs best for gait in Parkinson's disease: a 2013 meta-analysis concluded that auditory cueing is more effective for treating gait disorders in PD, a 2026 network meta-analysis reported somatosensory and visual cues as the most effective modalities for gait velocity and stride length, and the APTA guideline states, of reductions in motor disease severity when different modes of external cueing were compared, that no one mode of external cueing is superior to another. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23127307/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] The APTA guideline states that physical therapists should implement gait training to reduce motor disease severity and improve stride length, gait speed, mobility, and balance in individuals with PD (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong) and that there was no single gait training intervention that demonstrated greater improvement than other types of gait training; two randomized trials comparing robotic gait training with treadmill training each concluded that robotic gait training was not superior (one randomly allocated 30 patients to treadmill or Lokomat gait training and, at the 6-month follow-up, found no significant differences between the 2 groups, P =.53; Picelli et al. randomly assigned sixty patients with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease into three groups). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline on physical therapist management of Parkinson disease was published in Physical Therapy (2021 Dec 28;102(4):pzab302); its page carries a correction (Phys Ther. 2022 Aug 27;102(8):pzac098) about an author's affiliation and a later Editor's Note (Physical Therapy, 2024;104:pzae031) stating that Greek and Chinese translations of the article have been provided; and the guideline states that in 5 years it will either be revised by APTA, reaffirmed, or withdrawn. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] A 2014 Cochrane review (searches to 10 November 2013; two RCTs, 194 patients) reported no clear evidence of an effect of creatine on motor function (MD -0.26; 95% CI -4.39 to 3.88; low quality evidence) and judged the evidence base limited by risk of bias, small sample sizes and short duration, and a 2017 BMC Neurology meta-analysis (five RCTs, 1339 participants) reported no significant differences in total, mental, activities of daily living or motor UPDRS scores, with an improvement in Schwab & England Scale scores, and concluded that creatine has no observed benefit in PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10196714/
- [statement] The updated European evidence-based guidelines on rTMS (literature through the end of 2018; copyright 2019) assign Level B evidence (probable efficacy) to high-frequency rTMS of bilateral primary motor cortex regions for improving motor impairment in Parkinson's disease and to high-frequency rTMS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for improving depression in Parkinson's disease, and state that this does not mean the benefit inevitably reaches a level of clinical relevance. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31901449/
- [statement] Terkelsen et al. reported improved Lower Body and Gait scores at twelve months, during an open extension rather than a continued sham-controlled comparison; the authors explicitly state that a placebo effect on open-phase patient-reported improvements cannot be excluded. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w
- [statement] An rTMS meta-analysis of randomized trials searching through December 2024 included nineteen studies and 547 participants. It found benefits for freezing, gait speed and UPDRS-III, but not UPDRS total or TUG; publication-bias testing was positive for gait speed. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41517414/
- [statement] Liu et al. (2021) synthesized twenty-one tDCS studies involving 736 participants and concluded that evidence for motor improvement was insufficient; pooled UPDRS-III, Timed Up and Go, balance, and gait outcomes did not establish a motor benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8584149/
- [statement] rTMS has shown benefits for selected gait and motor outcomes in a randomized treadmill-training trial and a pooled analysis; benefit should be interpreted by outcome and stimulation protocol. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8470277/
- [statement] In a randomized trial of fifty-one participants, twelve sessions of 1Hz or 25Hz rTMS before treadmill training improved fastest walking speed more than sham at one day and three months; this evaluates rTMS as a rehabilitation adjunct. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8470277/
- [statement] Functional parkinsonism is assessed using positive examination signs such as effortful slowness without decrement, improvement with distraction, variable tremor, and active resistance during passive movement. (low confidence) — https://exonpublications.com/index.php/exon/article/view/191/349 · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Freezing is heterogeneous: OFF freezing usually improves with dopaminergic treatment, pseudo-ON freezing can improve with additional dopamine, and true ON freezing can be induced by dopaminergic stimulation; these categories should not be assumed to respond identically. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8592896/ · keywords: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
- [statement] For OFF-related freezing, reducing OFF time through individualized dopaminergic treatment is a first-line approach; the German guideline recommends levodopa for symptomatic freezing treatment. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8592896/ · keywords: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
- [statement] NINDS describes the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia as the main regions affected by CBD. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/corticobasal-degeneration · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] NICE recommends speech and language therapy for Parkinson’s disease when communication, swallowing or saliva problems occur; therapy includes swallowing safety strategies such as EMST and effort-based speech strategies. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] SIAXI’s population was 70.7% PD, so its overall results are not PD-only estimates. Treatment-related dry mouth occurred in 5.4% and 2.7%, and dysphagia in 2.7% and 0.0%, of the 75 U and 100 U groups respectively; these findings do not imply swallowing risk is absent. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30918101/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] In the 2010 blinded sham-controlled trial, 60 participants with PD completed four weeks of EMST or sham training; active EMST improved videofluoroscopic penetration–aspiration scores and hyolaryngeal function compared with sham. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2995389/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] In PD COMM, 388 people with PD and dysarthria were randomized. LSVT LOUD used four 50-minute sessions weekly for four weeks plus home practice, and reduced self-reported voice handicap at three months versus no therapy by 8.0 points (99% confidence interval −13.3 to −2.6). (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] PD COMM recorded 93 adverse events with LSVT LOUD and 46 with NHS speech and language therapy, predominantly vocal strain, with no serious adverse events. Most participants had early PD and mild speech impairment; allocation was unblinded and participant or carer expectations could bias questionnaire outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] In a sham-controlled randomized trial, 60 participants completed four weeks of EMST or sham training; EMST improved penetration–aspiration scores and hyolaryngeal function. NICE includes EMST among swallowing safety strategies. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2995389/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] In the 2012 multicenter placebo-controlled depression trial, paroxetine and venlafaxine XR improved depressive symptoms without worsening motor function; this describes that trial rather than proving all SSRIs effective in PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3324323/
- [statement] The 2024 German guideline says physical interventions might be offered for apathy, but its evidence discussion describes small mixed trials, including no significant dance-therapy effect versus active controls. Apathy exercise evidence is less established than a broad efficacy claim would imply. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/
- [statement] In the 48-participant anxiety CBT trial, CBT did not significantly outperform clinical monitoring on the primary Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale endpoint, although it improved the PD-specific Parkinson Anxiety Scale; benefit should be described as outcome-dependent. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/
- [statement] A single-center sham-controlled trial of motor-cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation reported a favorable musculoskeletal-pain signal in PD; its small sample and short follow-up support a preliminary adjunctive-treatment claim rather than broad efficacy across PD pain types. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32980772/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] A 2023 systematic review searching trials through May 2021 found a small fatigue benefit from physical exercise across eight trials, but called for further efficacy research and differentiation of physical versus mental fatigue outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10473113/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] In that 2023 review, pooled modafinil trials did not show a significant fatigue benefit versus placebo, and acupuncture did not show a significant advantage over sham acupuncture; these comparisons should not be presented as proven PD-fatigue therapies. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10473113/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Real acupuncture did not outperform sham acupuncture for PD fatigue in the Kluger and Kong randomized trials; a 2026 review likewise characterized fatigue evidence as very uncertain and without superiority over sham. Within-group improvement should not be presented as treatment-specific efficacy. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] The ACCORD-PD pilot found greater insomnia improvement among computerized CBT-I completers than education completers, but not in intention-to-treat analysis; dropout in the CBT-I group was 43%. Adherence limits generalizability. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5568719/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness

## Parkinson's disease surgical and device therapies: deep brain stimulation, adaptive DBS, focused ultrasound, levodopa pumps and infusions, and neuromodulation for gait
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-surgical-and-device-therapies-deep-brain-stimulation-adaptive-dbs-focused-ultrasound-levodopa-pumps-and-infusions-and-neuromodulation-for-gait"></a>

- [statement] The FDA February 28, 2025 roundup reported marketing approval of a software update providing adaptive DBS that adjusts stimulation from detected brain signals. The roundup described use in levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease with symptoms inadequately controlled by medication for at least four years; this historical announcement should not substitute for current device-specific labeling. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-28) — https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-roundup-february-28-2025 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] FDA's PMA database record for Medtronic supplement P960009/S478 (Activa, Percept and SenSight Deep Brain Stimulation Therapy System) lists a decision date of 02/20/2025 and an approval order statement for a new optional programming feature called adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS), within the indication of adjunctive therapy for levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease of at least 4 years' duration that is not adequately controlled with medication. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpma/pma.cfm?id=P960009S478 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] Adaptive DBS adjusts stimulation amplitude using neural feedback; the beta-band dual-threshold approach adjusts amplitude according to subthalamic local-field-potential power. (high confidence) — https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-roundup-february-28-2025 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] Two FDA documents give different dates for the aDBS approval: the PMA database lists a decision date of 02/20/2025 for supplement P960009/S478, while the FDA Roundup of February 28, 2025 says that on Friday, February 21 the FDA approved for marketing a software update to Medtronic's Activa, Percept and SenSight DBS system that adds adaptive deep brain stimulation. The one-day difference is recorded as an attributed discrepancy and is not resolved here. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpma/pma.cfm?id=P960009S478 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] The 2026 referral consensus states that the degree of symptom responsiveness to levodopa should be assessed and considered but should not be the only criterion for candidacy; a 2020 selection review recommends the levodopa challenge test as a key presurgical tool, states that the rule of UPDRS part-III improvement greater than 30% should not be strictly applied, and notes that patients with disabling dopa-resistant tremor could represent an exception. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01241-3
- [statement] When substantial dopaminergic medication reduction is the main surgical goal, evidence and the CNS guideline favor STN over GPi; medication reduction remains an individualized objective. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/
- [statement] Complete withdrawal of dopaminergic medication after STN DBS is discouraged in the programming review because a hypodopaminergic state can cause apathy and depression, sometimes delayed for weeks; medication adjustment and stimulation adjustment should be coordinated. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558426/
- [statement] The 2026 referral consensus states that gait impairment, freezing of gait and imbalance should not be the primary indications for surgery, that the risk of potential worsening of balance should be discussed with patients pre-operatively, and that DBS is unlikely to improve speech and speech impairment is a potential side effect of stimulation. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01241-3
- [statement] A 2025 review of DBS selection and programming states that programming begins once lead placement is confirmed and hardware integrity is ensured through an impedance check, that programming usually begins 3 to 4 weeks after lead implantation because microlesion effects can cause transient motor improvement, and that brief programming sessions can capture acute side effects but may fail to identify the full range of side effects that emerge with chronic stimulation. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01015-x
- [statement] The 2022 EAN/MDS-ES guideline on invasive therapies states that GPi-DBS can also be offered for advanced Parkinson's disease with fluctuations, that for early Parkinson's disease with early fluctuations STN-DBS is likely to improve motor symptoms and quality of life and can be offered, and that DBS should not be offered to people with early Parkinson's disease without fluctuations. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35791766/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The INVEST publication is a protocol for a planned open-label randomized comparison of DBS and continuous intrajejunal levodopa, with ancillary preference cohorts and quality-of-life and economic outcomes. Its planned sample and methods must not be cited as completed efficacy or cost-effectiveness results. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6995127/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Important burdens differ by modality: apomorphine can cause skin nodules, nausea and hypotension; intestinal levodopa can cause tube obstruction or displacement and abdominal complications; subcutaneous foslevodopa can cause infusion-site reactions or infections; DBS carries surgical and hardware risks. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2013 expert review states that very few comparative studies have evaluated the three device-aided therapies for specific motor problems and identifies the type of motor problems, age, and cognitive and psychiatric status as variables relevant to choosing among DBS, apomorphine infusion and duodenal/jejunal levodopa infusion. A 2024 review of advanced therapies states that there is no age limit for LCIG/LECIG and CSAI while an age limit for DBS is often discussed, that dementia is a clear contraindication for CSAI and DBS, that severe orthostatic hypotension and severe psychosis are contraindications for CSAI, and that frequent falls with injuries might be a contraindication for DBS. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3825542/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Apparent differences between device therapies in observational comparisons require caution: baseline differences can confound outcomes, and retrospective matching cannot remove all selection effects. The 2025 cohort also lacked systematic safety-data collection, preventing a full benefit-risk comparison. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10310730/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] NICE's topic-prioritisation page for levodopa/carbidopa (ND0612) for Parkinson's disease [ID6727] records the decision "Not selected" with a decision publication date of 25 November 2026; the topic had been selected for technology appraisal in December 2025 and was deselected because the product is not a new active substance or a significant licence extension. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-25) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/awaiting-development/gid-ta11954 · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2019 meta-analysis of five cohort studies involving 257 patients found no significant LCIG-versus-STN-DBS difference in UPDRS-III motor scores or adverse events; UPDRS-IV improvement favored STN-DBS, with substantial heterogeneity. Lack of significance does not establish equivalence. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6718716/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] In that foslevodopa-foscarbidopa trial, adverse events caused premature discontinuation in 16 of 74 infusion participants (22%) versus one of 67 oral-treatment participants (1%); infusion-site events were common. These trial-specific rates should not be used as a cross-device safety league table. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36402160/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2026 systematic review pooling subcutaneous levodopa and foslevodopa regimens found clinically meaningful OFF-time improvement versus oral levodopa, but patient-experience gains were statistically rather than clinically significant, with more infusion-site adverse events; these findings do not compare the pumps directly with DBS. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853972/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2024 review associates intestinal levodopa therapies with tube displacement, wound problems or infections, abdominal pain and polyneuropathy. It describes apomorphine infusion-site nodules, nausea, somnolence and possible impulse-control disorders; these are therapy-specific risks rather than a single common device-risk profile. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2025 retrospective cohort compared 295 people continuing oral therapy with 313 transitioning to device-aided therapy, including 284 DBS and 29 enteral levodopa recipients. Mean 12-month PDQ-39 summary-index change was −5.0 in the device group versus +0.9 in the oral group; these are pooled observational outcomes, not a randomized pump-versus-DBS comparison. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01093-x · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2025 study authors interpret their pooled cohort as showing meaningful quality-of-life improvement after device therapy. Zheng and Liu’s 2026 commentary accepts the observed improvement but questions causal interpretation because of residual candidacy confounding, differing baseline definitions and pooling DBS with enteral levodopa. The commentary identifies possible bias rather than proving the benefits are absent. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01093-x · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Delivery route changes invasiveness: subcutaneous apomorphine or levodopa avoids the intestinal tube procedure, intestinal levodopa requires a PEG-J system, and DBS requires intracranial electrode implantation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Intestinal levodopa bypasses gastric emptying to provide more stable plasma levodopa levels than oral dosing; subcutaneous levodopa is another continuous delivery strategy that avoids surgical jejunal tube placement. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Reviews of device-assisted therapy state that device selection depends on individual patient factors such as age, comorbidities, therapy-specific risks and patient preferences, and a single-centre comparison lists treatment availability, cost of treatment and local expertise as further considerations. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] External pumps require daily preparation and site or tube care, often with caregiver support; DBS exchanges this daily external-pump burden for neurosurgery and continuing device follow-up. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592668/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2023 non-randomised single-centre comparison included 66 patients (13 apomorphine, 19 LCIG, 34 STN-DBS); DBS recipients had better baseline profiles. Quality-of-life and motor outcomes improved with LCIG and DBS, while apomorphine changes were not statistically significant. The baseline imbalance prevents a causal treatment ranking. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10310730/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] OFF-time reduction alone does not guarantee a clinically important quality-of-life gain; this distinction appears in subcutaneous levodopa synthesis and long-term apomorphine experience. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853972/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Intestinal levodopa gel bypasses swallowing and gastric passage through a jejunal tube and an external pump; DBS requires implantation of electrodes and a pulse generator. Subcutaneous apomorphine and foslevodopa/foscarbidopa avoid the implantation surgery required for these other approaches. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2024 individualized-treatment review describes foslevodopa/foscarbidopa as a soluble prodrug formulation permitting continuous subcutaneous delivery over a 24-hour period. It reports infusion-site erythema, nodules, cellulitis and pain, as well as visual hallucinations, among adverse effects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Daily device work matters in treatment choice: LCIG and apomorphine pumps require cartridge changes and handling, often with relative or nursing support. DBS still requires specialist follow-up and rechargeable systems require charging; discussions should include maintenance, lifestyle and caregiver needs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation reported on February 3, 2026 that ND0612, an under-the-skin infusion of levodopa and carbidopa, had received a second FDA Complete Response Letter; it states that the FDA sent a first Complete Response Letter in June 2024 and, after the company's May 2025 resubmission, issued the second in October 2025. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-03) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/news/second-fda-response-letter-issued-nd0612-therapy · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Disabling tremor that persists despite optimized medication can justify specialist assessment for invasive treatment, including deep brain stimulation; the tremor review also identifies focused ultrasound as an option. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10041452/ · keywords: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
- [statement] FDA’s safety summary identifies adaptive deep brain stimulation as device supplement P960009/S478 and dates its approval notice February 20, 2025; FDA’s roundup describes marketing approval on February 21. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-28) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf · keywords: Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies
- [statement] Deep learning is not uniformly superior: a review of deep learning in PD reports state-of-the-art performance in many PD-related tasks by outperforming conventional machine learning approaches, while a gait meta-analysis reports that ML models achieved the best results for classifying healthy patients (H&Y0: 95.7% to 98.2%) and DL approaches performed better for classifying higher severity levels (>92%). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37200116/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] In WATCH-PD, the authors report that device-derived features, particularly arm swing, the proportion of time with tremor, and finger tapping, differed significantly between individuals with early PD and age-matched controls and had variable correlation with traditional assessments. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108794/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] The authors report that at 18 months after grafting putaminal 18Fluoro-DOPA positron emission tomography uptake increased, which they interpret as indicating graft survival. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] REGENERATE-PD (NCT06285643) is registered as a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, sham surgery-controlled study of intraputaminal AAV2-GDNF in adults with moderate stage Parkinson's disease. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06285643 · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] In the phase 2 randomised trial of bilateral AAV2-GAD delivery in the subthalamic nucleus in advanced Parkinson's disease, the primary outcome measure was the 6-month change from baseline in double-blind assessment of off-medication UPDRS motor scores. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21419704/ · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] In a double-blind trial of AAV2-neurturin delivered to the putamen and substantia nigra in advanced Parkinson disease, the authors report no significant difference between groups in the primary endpoint (change from baseline: AAV2-neurturin, -7.0 ± 9.92; sham, -5.2 ± 10.01; p = 0.515) among Fifty-one patients, and conclude that it was not superior to sham surgery. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26061140/ · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] The authors report that all participants experienced treatment-emergent AE, most of them transient and perioperative, and that serious AEs (n=5) were unrelated to AAV2-GDNF in this early-phase study. (low confidence) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000206690 · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] In the AAV-hAADC study of bilateral intraputaminal infusion in patients with moderately advanced PD, with low-dose and high-dose cohorts of 5 patients in each, the authors report the gene therapy was well tolerated, but 1 symptomatic and 2 asymptomatic intracranial hemorrhages followed the operative procedure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2839805/ · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] Mobility-aid selection should involve qualified professionals and assessment of the individual’s physical, attention and executive-function abilities. Evidence remains insufficient to identify a universally best PD walking aid. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9631832/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] In a randomized controlled trial funded by the National Institutes of Health and LSVT Global, Inc. (several authors report employment or consulting roles with LSVT Global), 64 participants with Parkinson's disease were randomized to LSVT LOUD, LSVT ARTIC or no treatment; sound pressure level (the primary outcome) improved more with LSVT LOUD than with LSVT ARTIC or no treatment at 1 and 7 months, while between-group differences in the participant-reported CETI-M were not significant at 7 months (P = 0.08). (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261685/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] Two speech-therapy guidance documents name LSVT: the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists' Parkinson's guidance (last updated December 2025) states that LSVT LOUD is highly recommended for communication problems in people with Parkinson's, calls it the only behavioural treatment with strong evidence for managing dysarthria (supported by 40 studies), and recommends telehealth in specific well-defined treatments such as LSVT LOUD; the Dutch guideline for speech-language therapy in Parkinson's disease (Dutch text published in 2008; English edition copyright 2011) strongly recommends PLVT or LSVT for people with hypokinetic dysarthria who satisfy the indications for intensive treatment. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.rcslt.org/members/clinical-guidance/parkinsons/parkinsons-guidance/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
