- [statement] Two meta-analyses of randomized trials report greater vocal intensity (sound pressure level) after LSVT than with control interventions: one pooled 141 participants and found a higher level with LSVT of 7.36 dB (95% CI 6.60-8.12) immediately after treatment, and the other reported increases of 8.87, 4.34, 3.25 and 3.31 dB for sustained 'Ah' phonation, Rainbow passage reading, monologue and picture description after one month versus no intervention; both sets of authors state that larger randomized trials are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8782619/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] In a published comparison table of the two programmes, LSVT LOUD directs increased movement amplitude predominately to the respiratory/laryngeal systems whereas LSVT BIG directs it across the limb motor system including gait; the Berlin LSVT BIG study report describes LSVT BIG as focusing on intensive exercising of high-amplitude movements. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] Randomised trials of remote delivery of LSVT LOUD report outcomes comparable to face-to-face delivery: Constantinescu and colleagues confirmed non-inferiority of online delivery for the primary outcome (mean change in sound pressure level on a monologue task); Theodoros and colleagues, in a single-blinded noninferiority trial (31 participants randomly assigned to face-to-face or online treatment, plus 21 non-metropolitan participants treated online), confirmed noninferiority of online treatment; and a 2025 pilot trial of 20 people comparing teletherapy with face-to-face LSVT LOUD concluded that both appear effective and that larger studies are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21281410/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] On technology-delivered cueing, a technological review of wearable cueing systems for freezing of gait states that novel cueing systems have been evaluated predominantly in laboratory settings, a narrative review states that the increasing use of wearable technology is allowing the cue type, cue content and dose to be adapted to individual patients, and the APTA guideline notes that the cost of utilizing technology for the external cueing source should be considered. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6470562/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] The FDA summary of safety and effectiveness for P960009/S478 states that the aDBS feature has been marketed for Parkinson's disease in Japan with the Percept PC since May 2020 and the Percept RC since November 2022, and in Europe with both models since January 2025. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] The registry record for NCT07398157, a University of California, San Francisco interventional trial titled "Simplified, Scalable, 24-hour Adaptive DBS in Parkinson's Disease", lists overall status RECRUITING (status verified 2026-09), an actual start date of 2026-04-09, an estimated enrollment of 24 and an estimated primary completion date of 2029-11-30; its summary says researchers will compare study-derived adaptive DBS settings with clinically programmed continuous DBS settings. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT07398157 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] Oehrn and colleagues reported improved motor symptoms and quality of life versus clinically optimized continuous DBS in a blinded randomized crossover feasibility trial involving four male patients. Their personalized feedback markers were stimulation-entrained gamma oscillations in the subthalamic nucleus or motor cortex; the authors called for larger trials. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826929/ · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] ADAPT-PD enrolled 68 participants previously stable on continuous DBS and medication. Its comparison of adaptive versus continuous DBS was open-label; randomization and blinding compared the two adaptive modes in participants tolerating both. The study therefore does not establish blinded randomized superiority of adaptive over continuous DBS. (low confidence) — https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2839117 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] In ADAPT-PD, the post hoc primary performance threshold was met by 91% receiving dual-threshold and 79% receiving single-threshold adaptive DBS. This measured preservation of good on-time relative to continuous DBS rather than a superiority endpoint. Single-threshold treatment reduced total electrical energy delivered by 15%; this was not a measured 15% battery-longevity extension. (low confidence) — https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2839117 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] In a randomized double-blind crossover assessment of directional versus omnidirectional stimulation, directional stimulation widened the therapeutic window in 183 of 202 evaluable participants (90.6%), with a mean increase of 41%. Therapeutic window denotes stimulation amplitudes achieving symptom relief without side effects; the study enrolled 234 subjects. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34047410/ · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] A separate 19-patient randomized directional-versus-omnidirectional crossover trial found no significant differences in primary rigidity or secondary clinical motor outcomes. Its discussion reported 30% lower stimulation intensity with directional stimulation, while chronic motor performance could worsen under the tested directional settings. Wider therapeutic windows should not be equated with universally superior motor outcomes. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00812-0 · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] The comparative adaptive-DBS literature is heterogeneous: Oehrn and colleagues reported benefit in their four-person personalized gamma-feedback feasibility trial, whereas a nine-person beta-feedback crossover pilot reported no significant treatment differences. These are attributed results from different protocols and populations, not an interchangeable estimate of efficacy. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826929/ · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] The FDA summary of safety and effectiveness for P960009/S478 states that aDBS was not studied in the ADAPT-PD trial with bilaterally implanted neurostimulators, that only subjects with single implanted neurostimulators were eligible, and that the labeling instructs clinicians not to use aDBS with more than one implanted neurostimulator. (low confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf · keywords: Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads
- [statement] A 2020 selection review describes levodopa-resistant axial symptoms as a relative contraindication for surgery, while the 2026 referral consensus states that axial symptoms and freezing of gait should not be the sole indication for DBS but, when levodopa-responsive and associated with disabling motor fluctuations, may benefit from appropriately targeted and individualized DBS approaches and should not be viewed as absolute contraindications to surgery. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7761824/
- [statement] A programming review states that rigidity is typically used to judge the effect of STN-DBS because it does not fluctuate, responds to stimulation adjustments within seconds and does not depend on patient fatigue or cooperation, that no single clinical sign should be used alone to judge the therapeutic effect, and that the contact with the lowest threshold for beneficial effects and the widest therapeutic window is then selected for chronic stimulation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558426/
- [statement] The 2026 expert consensus on referral for DBS states that patients with Parkinson's disease supported by the IPMDS clinical diagnostic criteria should be considered for DBS surgery evaluation in situations that include troublesome motor fluctuations and/or dyskinesia that interfere with functioning or quality of life despite optimal medical management, or disabling tremor that is refractory to an adequate levodopa trial. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01241-3
- [statement] The 2026 referral consensus states that pre-DBS assessments should include neurological, neurosurgical and neuropsychological evaluations and discussion of the patient's and family's goals and expectations, and that evaluation by an interdisciplinary team is the optimal approach for selecting DBS candidates; a review of patient and target selection adds that preoperative neuropsychiatric and neuropsychological assessment is necessary for risk stratification and that psychiatric clinical stability and social support should be determined before surgery. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01241-3
- [statement] The 2026 referral consensus states that evidence exists that patients with cognitive impairment may still benefit from DBS for motor symptoms, that there is no data-driven cognitive-performance cut-off for considering DBS, and that mood, anxiety and other psychiatric disturbances do not necessarily exclude candidacy while significant psychiatric symptoms identified by the interdisciplinary team should be addressed prior to surgery. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01241-3
- [statement] For conventional ring-contact programming, monopolar review tests contacts individually with the lead contact as cathode and pulse-generator case as anode, identifying benefit and adverse-effect thresholds to select a therapeutic window. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558426/
- [statement] Either STN or GPi can be selected for motor benefit; in the randomized trial’s 36-month follow-up, motor improvement was sustained and comparable between targets. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/
- [statement] Device-aided therapy is considered when oral or transdermal treatment inadequately controls disabling motor fluctuations or dyskinesia; options include apomorphine infusion, intestinal levodopa infusion, subcutaneous levodopa infusion and DBS. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3825542/
- [statement] The 2024 pallidotomy meta-analysis pooled post-treatment changes against baseline in a single-arm analysis because it could not compare against a sham/control group. Its pooled improvements therefore should not be interpreted as sham-adjusted treatment effects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11422448/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Thalamotomy can cause persistent neurological deficits. The randomized trial reported persistent paresthesia and ataxia, and the prescriber information describes serious hemiparesis linked to edema and lesion extension toward the internal capsule. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822192/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Focused ultrasound thalamotomy is an ablative treatment directed at medication-refractory tremor in tremor-dominant Parkinson disease; pallidotomy targets GPi for motor complications, including dyskinesia. (high confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf15/P150038S037B.pdf · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] FDA supplement S014, decided October 29, 2021, approved unilateral Exablate Neuro pallidotomy as an adjunct to medication for advanced idiopathic Parkinson disease with medication-refractory moderate to severe motor complications, age at least 30. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpma/pma.cfm?id=P150038S014 · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] The 2022 EAN/MDS-ES guideline on invasive therapies states that unilateral MRgFUS of the STN can be considered for distinctly unilateral Parkinson's disease within registries, and its clinical-consensus statements say that unilateral MRgFUS of the thalamus for medication-resistant tremor of Parkinson's disease can be considered only within registries. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35791766/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] In the 27-patient pilot randomized thalamotomy trial, the on-medication treated-hand tremor subscore improved a median 62% after ultrasound versus 22% after sham at 3 months; this is a score reduction, not a percentage of patients cured. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822192/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] The pallidotomy randomized trial enrolled 94 patients; 65 active-treatment and 22 control patients completed primary assessment. At 3 months, 45 (69%) versus 7 (32%) responded. Response meant at least a 3-point reduction in treated-side off-medication MDS-UPDRS III or on-medication UDysRS, rather than requiring both. (low confidence) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202721 · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] The FDA thalamotomy labeling specifies unilateral ventral intermediate thalamic treatment for medication-refractory tremor in tremor-dominant Parkinson’s disease, in patients at least age 30; it is a tremor indication rather than an indication for all Parkinsonian symptoms. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf15/P150038S006D.pdf · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Sources differ on unilateral focused ultrasound pallidotomy for Parkinson's disease: the 2022 EAN/MDS-ES guideline's clinical-consensus statement says that unilateral MRgFUS of the pallidum is not recommended, whereas the FDA PMA record for Exablate Neuro lists approval of unilateral pallidotomy for advanced idiopathic Parkinson's disease with a decision date of 10/29/2021, and the NEJM sham-controlled trial reports a response in 45 patients (69%) after ablation versus 7 (32%) after sham. The sources carry different dates, evidence bases and jurisdictions and are recorded side by side, not reconciled. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35791766/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Thalamotomy trial safety findings included two cases of mild hemiparesis from internal-capsule heating that improved, alongside persistent orofacial paresthesia, finger paresthesia and ataxia. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822192/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Pallidotomy durability was assessed in an open-label extension: 30 of 39 assessed initial responders still responded at 12 months. This denominator excludes initial nonresponders and unassessed responders. (low confidence) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202721 · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Pallidotomy-related adverse events included dysarthria, gait disturbance, loss of taste, visual disturbance and facial weakness; investigators called for longer and larger trials. (medium confidence) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202721 · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] The July 3, 2025 FDA S037 expansion concerns pallidothalamic tractotomy, including a contralateral procedure staged at least 6 months later in eligible patients aged at least 30. It must not be described as blanket approval of bilateral GPi pallidotomy or bilateral Parkinson thalamotomy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-03) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf15/P150038S037B.pdf · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] NICE HTG733, published December 18, 2024, restricts focused ultrasound thalamotomy for moderate-to-severe Parkinson’s tremor to formal research approved by a research ethics committee. That NHS recommendation is jurisdiction-specific and should be distinguished from FDA device approval. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-12-18) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg733/chapter/1-Recommendations · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy are lesioning procedures: focused acoustic energy heats and ablates a selected brain target, with MRI thermometry and clinical testing guiding delivery. Incisionless delivery still entails destruction of brain tissue. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf15/P150038S006D.pdf · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Patient selection requires more than symptom severity: the tremor-dominant Parkinson’s prescriber information requires MRI suitability, ability to tolerate and communicate during treatment, and screening for bleeding risks, prolonged immobilization and skull-density constraints. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf15/P150038S006D.pdf · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] A double-blind randomized trial of multitarget tDCS (abstract copyright 2021) enrolled seventy-seven participants with Parkinson disease and freezing; it did not improve the primary laboratory freezing-provoking test, although secondary self-reported freezing and daily step-count outcomes favored stimulation and a milder-freezing subgroup showed signals warranting further investigation. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34406695/
- [statement] SCS implantation carries procedural risks: Terkelsen et al. reported four serious adverse events related to implantation, comprising dural puncture, two lead misplacements, and perioperative pain; dural puncture and lead misplacement required repeat surgery. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w
- [statement] A randomized double-blind sham-controlled trial (abstract copyright 2019) allocated thirty patients with freezing of gait to ten sessions of real or sham 10 Hz rTMS over the supplementary motor area; ON-medication assessments showed improvements in freezing questionnaire, motor, and gait outcomes during follow-up through four weeks. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31689588/
- [statement] Implanted SCS delivers electrical stimulation through an epidural lead connected to a subcutaneous pulse generator; its use for Parkinsonian gait is distinct from its established pain indication. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/
- [statement] Evidence reviewed here does not establish reliable tDCS benefit for Parkinsonian motor function: a randomized freezing-of-gait trial missed its primary endpoint and a 2021 systematic review found insufficient motor-function evidence. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34406695/
- [statement] A predominantly lower-limb gait syndrome can suggest vascular parkinsonism, but cerebrovascular imaging abnormalities are not conclusive because vascular disease and PD may coexist. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is another potentially treatable mimic with gait, urinary and cognitive symptoms and ventriculomegaly. (low confidence) — https://exonpublications.com/index.php/exon/article/view/191/349 · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] NICE advises against deep brain stimulation when best medical therapy adequately controls symptoms, and recommends considering it when advanced disease is not adequately controlled; the MDS review also describes escalation when less invasive options provide insufficient benefit. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management
- [statement] The methylphenidate gait trial report states that dopaminergic treatments and currently available surgical therapies are often insufficiently effective for gait disorders in PD, and NICE NG71 recommends offering Parkinson's disease-specific physiotherapy for people experiencing balance or motor function problems. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068005/ · keywords: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
- [statement] Rocha and colleagues describe the hyperdirect pathway as excitatory cerebral cortex projections to the STN that reinforce basal ganglia inhibitory output. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] Rocha and colleagues describe basal ganglia output nuclei as influencing descending motor pathways as well as the thalamo-cortical pathway. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] The 2019 MDS review rated clozapine and pimavanserin clinically useful for PD psychosis; the 2024 systematic review of reviews also identified these two agents as having the strongest efficacy and tolerability evidence. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/
- [statement] Small experimental studies found that levodopa can increase pain thresholds in PD. These laboratory threshold results should be distinguished from demonstrated relief of chronic clinical pain. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16078219/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Experimental findings on sensory thresholds conflict: one study reported that thermal and mechanical pain thresholds were uninfluenced by levodopa or STN-DBS, whereas another reported significant increases in mechanical pain and tolerance thresholds after acute STN-DBS and after acute levodopa administration. A uniform direct effect on central pain processing is not established by these studies. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20629160/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms

## Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-lifestyle-and-supportive-care-diet-and-nutrition-caffeine-falls-and-home-safety-daily-living-cbt-and-cognitive-training-palliative-care-care-partners-and-care-models"></a>

- [statement] A varied whole-food diet that supplies adequate energy and protein is practical supportive care in PD; a Mediterranean-style pattern is a reasonable default, while meals should be individualized with a dietitian to nutritional needs and medication timing. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/diet-nutrition
- [statement] The 2026 alcohol review explicitly advises that neither alcohol consumption nor smoking can be recommended for PD prevention because of their overall health harms. Apparent inverse epidemiologic associations should not be translated into advice to start either exposure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13067329/
- [statement] Observational associations require consideration of confounding and reverse causation, including changes in exposure during prodromal PD. Courage-PD used genetic instruments to address these biases and supported an inverse smoking association, while explicitly leaving coffee and alcohol conclusions uncertain because of limited power. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/
- [statement] In Café-PD, 121 people with established PD were randomized to caffeine 200 mg twice daily or placebo. Caffeine did not significantly improve the primary motor outcome at six months; early modest sleepiness improvement attenuated over time, and secondary outcomes included slightly worse cognitive scores and increased dyskinesia. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/
- [statement] A 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association, but associations differed by CYP1A2 genotype: below 5 cups/day was associated with lower risk in AA carriers, whereas at least 5 cups/day was associated with higher risk in AC and CC carriers. The authors explicitly describe these observational findings as hypothesis-generating and noncausal. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0
- [statement] Lower PD incidence associated with coffee consumption should be distinguished from treating established PD: EPIC4PD observed an inverse risk association, while Café-PD found no clinically important motor benefit from caffeine treatment. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] Prospective observational evidence frequently associates habitual caffeine or coffee consumption with lower incident PD risk: the 2020 cohort meta-analysis reported HR 0.797 (95% CI 0.748–0.849), and EPIC4PD also reported an inverse association. These are risk associations rather than intervention effects. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7353179/
- [statement] In the 2024 EPIC4PD analysis of 184,024 participants, the highest coffee-intake category versus nonconsumption had adjusted HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.46–0.88). Its nested study of 351 incident cases and 351 controls associated higher prediagnostic caffeine, paraxanthine and theophylline with lower subsequent PD risk; adjustment for smoking and alcohol did not substantially change results. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] In Café-PD, caffeine 200 mg twice daily did not improve the six-month motor outcome versus placebo in established PD. Sixty participants received caffeine and 61 placebo; the between-group MDS-UPDRS-III difference was −0.48 points (95% CI −3.21 to 2.25). This treatment result does not test primary prevention. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/
- [statement] The 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association in 435,551 participants with 3319 incident cases, whereas EPIC4PD reported an inverse association. The UK analysis reported differing associations by CYP1A2 genotype; these study-specific results should not be collapsed into a universal protective coffee effect. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0
- [statement] In the UK Biobank study, coffee-by-CYP1A2 interaction was significant, but coffee-by-sex and the three-way coffee-by-genotype-by-sex interactions were not statistically significant. Sex-stratified differences therefore require caution. The authors also state that their coffee measure included decaffeinated coffee, preventing isolation of caffeine-specific exposure, and that this observational study does not establish causality. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0
- [statement] Burden scales can structure assessment: the 2024 meta-analysis identified the ZBI as the most used measure, and the 2025 predictor review also found it used more often than the other listed scales. Scores should be interpreted alongside the caregiver’s own account because validated measures may miss aspects of lived experience. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A Parkinson’s News Today feature describes irritability, exhaustion and low patience as burnout warning signs and illustrates the value one care partner places on specific offers of practical help. This is a reported personal experience and support guidance, not a validated diagnostic rule or causal trial. (low confidence) — https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/avoiding-parkinsons-care-partner-burnout/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] The evidence base underrepresents some care partners: the 2025 review calls for younger and non-spousal caregivers and more diverse samples, while its limitations describe predominantly older female spouses and recruitment biased toward outpatient settings. Generalization to all caregiver relationships and disease stages requires caution. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A patient-education RCT involving 46 care partners found short-term improvements in psychosocial problems and need for help after eight weekly sessions. A separate formative evaluation found improvements in those domains but none on health-state, quality-of-life or depression measures; outcomes should be reported by domain rather than as a blanket improvement in well-being. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19674927/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Caregiver burden describes adverse effects on caregivers’ physical, emotional, social and financial well-being; it should be assessed as the care partner’s own experience rather than equated with the person with PD being a burden. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Practical support should address the care partner’s own unmet needs, including psychosocial help and opportunities for respite; these are support priorities described in the literature, rather than a guarantee that any particular service will reduce burden. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Care partner burden in PD encompasses effects on emotional and physical health, social participation and finances; caregiving can also be rewarding, so burden should not be assumed to define every relationship. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Caregiver mental health warrants assessment in its own right: a cross-sectional baseline analysis of 175 patient-caregiver pairs associated caregiver depression and anxiety with burden, and a 2025 systematic review identified poorer caregiver mental health among predictors. These are associations, not proof that treating anxiety alone reduces burden. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31735048/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] In interviews with 36 care partners across 11 European countries, participants described information needs distinct from those of the person with PD, especially medication management, side effects, contacts for problems and responses to behavioural or mental health symptoms. These qualitative findings describe needs, not intervention effectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10578036/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Practical support options include planned time away from caregiving, help from relatives or friends, social-work resource navigation and respite or in-home assistance; the Foundation recommends these options, and qualitative research documents care partners’ unmet need for time to themselves. This supports a needs-based support plan, without establishing a quantified treatment effect. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/blog/care/address-prevent-burnout · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Peer groups need a suitable format: the European interview study found mixed experiences, including reluctance to voice concerns in front of the person with PD; participants appreciated care-partner-specific groups. Generic support groups should not be assumed to meet everyone’s needs. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10578036/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] CBT evidence for care-partner burden is mixed: the preliminary Secker–Brown trial reported improvement, whereas a 2024 meta-analysis reported no significant pooled burden reduction. The positive small trial does not establish a reliable general effect, and the pooled null result does not prove that no individual can benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1739584/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation care-partner page directs readers to its Helpline, local chapters, support groups and free self-paced care-partner courses. These are resource-navigation options; the page is not trial evidence for reducing burden. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Care partnering includes emotional support as well as physical tasks, and the role changes as PD progresses; support planning should recognize this evolving involvement. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] In the PEPP randomized trial, sixty-four people with PD and 46 caregivers were allocated to education or usual care. Eight weekly 90-minute sessions improved caregivers’ psychosocial problems and need for help at assessment one week after completion; this short follow-up does not establish durable benefit. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19674927/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A survey of 141 current and 15 former PD carers identified unmet needs around finding balance, relationship changes, and coping with reduced emotions and motivation. About half of current carers were interested in exchanging experience with former carers, and commonality with peers mattered. This was a needs-and-preferences study, not a trial proving burden reduction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9569356/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Psychoeducation and other caregiver support interventions are promising, but reliable long-term burden reduction is not established across programs. The scoping review identified small samples, inconsistent outcomes and limited longitudinal data; the 2024 meta-analysis found no significant pooled caregiver-burden effect for cognitive behavior therapy. Improvement in mood or coping should not be described automatically as improvement in burden. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] At one- and two-year COGTIPS follow-up, cognitive training showed no advantage on neuropsychological outcomes or conversion of cognitive status compared with an active control. Missing assessments, particularly during COVID-19 restrictions, limit interpretation. The result concerns the studied eight-week program. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10724826/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] PD-adapted CBT can improve depressive and anxiety symptoms compared with usual care or other control conditions; trial effects should not be interpreted as proof that every patient benefits. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] PD-adapted CBT uses cognitive and behavioral coping skills. Depression protocols include behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring and anxiety management; anxiety protocols include psychoeducation, exposure, thought restructuring and home practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In Moonen and colleagues’ 48-person anxiety trial, ten weekly CBT sessions did not significantly outperform clinical monitoring on the primary Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. The secondary Parkinson Anxiety Scale favored CBT, so outcome choice materially affects interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] A stress-and-mindfulness viewpoint presented potential effects on PD progression as a hypothetical mechanistic framework informed partly by animal studies; this source does not demonstrate that mindfulness slows human PD progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894549/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Mediterranean and MIND patterns emphasize plant foods, olive oil, fish and nuts and discourage red meat and sweets. MIND scoring additionally emphasizes leafy greens, berries and whole grains and penalizes butter, cheese and fried foods; different scoring scales cannot be compared as equivalent dose units. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/
- [statement] A 2026 critical review concluded that no nutritional intervention had independently replicated, durable cognitive efficacy in established PD. It treats a Mediterranean-style pattern as a reasonable nutritional default rather than an established cognitive treatment. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708064/
- [statement] A single-center Mediterranean-diet trial randomized eighty people with idiopathic PD to diet or control for 10 weeks; 35 per group completed it. Its abstract reports improved total MoCA and several domains, with no significant change in some other domains. This is short-term cognitive testing, not evidence of prevented dementia. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32444045/
- [statement] The 2024 systematic review described promising dietary associations but acknowledged heterogeneous designs, frequent observational evidence, self-reported intake and limited long-term follow-up. A review of randomized trials found evidence inconclusive for improving PD progression, symptoms and severity; inconclusiveness is not proof that diets are ineffective. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11513219/
- [statement] The October 2026 cognition-focused critical narrative review concluded that no nutritional intervention had independently replicated, durable cognitive efficacy in established PD, and no included study showed durable functional benefit or reduced progression to dementia. This is the review’s time-bounded conclusion, not proof that all dietary approaches are ineffective. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708064/
- [statement] A small prospective observational study of 30 people with PD found fewer outdoor falls and fall injuries among rollator users. Participants used rollators only outdoors, and the study could not adjust for other factors because of its small sample; it does not establish causal protection, indoor benefit or superiority of a particular model. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9984883/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] In the PDSAFE randomized trial, the programme did not reduce falling overall, despite improvements in balance, falls efficacy and chair-stand time and fewer near falls. Secondary subgroup findings suggested different responses by disease severity. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] For stairs, the Parkinson’s Foundation recommends clear, non-skid, well-lit steps and handrails; it advises avoiding ladders, step stools and chairs for climbing because balance and protective reflex changes increase fall risk. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The 2022 Cochrane review found that exercise probably reduces fall rate in mild to moderate PD by 26% (rate ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.63–0.87; 1456 participants, 12 studies; moderate-certainty evidence). This describes falls per unit time, rather than a 26% reduction in the number of people who fall. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9169540/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Home exercise benefits cannot be assumed to extend unchanged to severe PD. PDSAFE and a separate minimally supervised exercise trial found severity-dependent responses; in the latter, the higher-severity subgroup had a nonsignificant trend toward more falls. Subgroup findings warrant caution rather than a claim that exercise invariably harms advanced PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9169540/
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends removing clutter and trip hazards, maintaining stable non-skid floors, improving lighting, creating wide walking paths, and keeping electrical cords out of walking routes. These are practical recommendations, rather than a quantified PD-specific intervention effect. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] In the PDSAFE randomized trial, repeat falling at six months did not significantly improve: 61.5% in the intervention group versus 55% in controls (controlled OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.74–1.98). Balance, falls efficacy and chair stand time improved despite the negative primary fall outcome. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Practical PD home-safety guidance recommends clearing clutter and loose rugs, keeping cords out of walking routes, providing good lighting and leaving wide paths for mobility aids. These are guidance recommendations; these pages do not establish a PD-specific numerical treatment effect. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends discussing an in-home occupational-therapy Home Safety Evaluation with the doctor to obtain personalized recommendations. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] External cueing can improve freezing and gait outcomes, but those improvements should not be equated with proven fall prevention. The APTA guideline recommends cueing yet reports no studies of cueing effects on fall rate or number of falls in its evidence review; the mobility-aid review calls for more free-living controlled studies. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation advises planning how to call a family member or emergency services after a fall, including discussion of assistive technology with the doctor and occupational therapist. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] In a Parkinson’s UK forum discussion, a participant described the importance of rollator brakes for public transport and handle-height adjustment. This is user experience that can inform assessment questions, not comparative evidence that a brand prevents falls. (low confidence) — https://forum.parkinsons.org.uk/t/linda-rollator-advice/42013 · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] For bathrooms, the Parkinson’s Foundation recommends grab bars near the toilet, tub and shower, an elevated toilet seat with support, and a sturdy shower or tub bench; towel racks and faucets should not serve as grab bars. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends accessible bedroom lighting and a nightlight for the route to the bathroom, and planning how to summon help after a fall. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] A 2022 mobility-aid review reported that some studies of canes and standard or two-wheeled walkers without visual cues found slower gait and shorter strides without significant improvement in freezing or falls. Visual or auditory cues improved some gait and freezing measures, but this does not establish reliable real-world fall prevention. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9631832/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation advises avoiding driving when fatigued, when medication is wearing off, or when starting a new medicine. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/driving · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] In a Parkinson’s UK forum discussion, one traveler with PD reported that advance wheelchair assistance helped with airport queues and walking; this is an individual experience rather than evidence that one itinerary is best for everyone. (low confidence) — https://forum.parkinsons.org.uk/t/long-distance-air-travel-uk-to-australia-advice-please/43760 · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] A PD diagnosis alone does not determine whether someone can drive safely; the Parkinson’s Foundation advises assessment of the individual’s symptoms and other age-related changes. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/driving · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] For time-zone travel, the Parkinson’s Foundation advises preserving the prescribed intervals between doses; Davis Phinney Foundation travel guidance likewise recommends planning a consistent medication schedule. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/traveling · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] How long a person continues working after PD diagnosis varies with job demands, symptoms and circumstances; Parkinson’s Europe describes contrasting personal experiences of continuing work and leaving work. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/employment · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] Occupational therapy can tailor routines and task strategies to a person’s priorities, including dressing, cooking, handwriting, work and driving; the plan is tested and adjusted to the person’s needs. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/occupational-therapy · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] Multidisciplinary PD care is a patient-centered, needs-based model involving different professionals; the Parkinson Foundation describes experts working as needed across symptoms, while one randomized specialist-team model combined a movement-disorders specialist, PD nurses, and a social worker. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Palliative care addresses symptoms, psychosocial concerns and future planning; NICE recommends considering referral at any stage of PD, so it need not wait until the terminal phase. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] NICE’s 2017 PD recommendations advise oral and written information about progression, future treatment options and end-of-life issues, with the discussion recorded; named UK planning mechanisms include ADRT, DNACPR and Lasting Power of Attorney. These are UK guideline examples, not universal legal instruments. (low confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] In the 2026 PD_Pal trial, 189 participants with advanced parkinsonism were randomized to a six-month nurse-led ACP and care-coordination intervention or usual care; documented end-of-life preferences did not differ significantly at six months (P=0.77). This trial does not establish that structured ACP universally improves documentation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771020/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] NICE recommends prognosis discussions that promote patient priorities and shared decisions, and recognition that relatives may have different information needs from the person with PD. (low confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] Systematic reviews of Nordic walking in Parkinson's disease differ in how they characterize benefit: Salse-Batán et al. (twelve studies) report that none of the statistically significant benefits were clinically meaningful except for walking ability and that Nordic Walking does not lead to clinically significant changes in global motor impairment, functional mobility, balance and physical fitness, whereas De Santis and Kaplan (13 studies, 318 patients) report that symptom severity, walking speed and gait pattern consistently improved after 4 to 24 weeks of Nordic walking relative to baseline or any control condition during ON-phases of pharmacotherapy, while rating study quality as poor to moderate. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35593147/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page states last reviewed 19 December 2024) recommends offering Parkinson's disease-specific physiotherapy to people experiencing balance or motor function problems (recommendation 1.7.3) and considering referral of people in the early stages to a physiotherapist with experience of Parkinson's disease (recommendation 1.7.2); the 2024 German Society for Neurology guideline states that people with PD and impairment from motor symptoms in everyday life should have access to physiotherapy treatment. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline and the Cochrane network meta-analysis state different certainty ratings for aerobic (endurance) exercise and for resistance training: APTA labels both with high evidence quality and strong recommendation strength, while the Cochrane review rates confidence as low for endurance training and for strength/resistance training on the severity of motor signs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Sources describe limited durability of cueing effects: the APTA guideline states that the lasting effects of cueing are unclear because benefits appear to dissipate over time, and that effects appear to dissipate when the cues are removed; the RESCUE crossover trial (153 patients; 3-week home cueing programme using a prototype cueing device) reported that effects of intervention had reduced considerably at 6-week follow-up; and a narrative review of cueing in people with freezing of gait reported that long-term consolidation and transfer of the effects appear to be hampered in that subgroup. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page records 'Last reviewed: 19 December 2024') includes recommendation 1.7.6, 'Offer Parkinson's disease-specific occupational therapy for people who are having difficulties with activities of daily living', and recommendation 1.7.5, which advises considering referral of people in the early stages of Parkinson's disease to an occupational therapist with experience of Parkinson's disease for assessment, education and advice on motor and non-motor symptoms; the 2022 American Occupational Therapy Association practice guideline states that 'Multidisciplinary, tailored, goal-oriented intervention is recommended for people with PD'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Two meta-analyses report improved walking speed with treadmill training in Parkinson's disease but no improvement in cadence: the Cochrane review (18 trials, 633 participants; last searched September 2014) reported improved gait speed (MD = 0.09 m/s; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.03 to 0.14; moderate quality of evidence) and that cadence did not improve (MD = 2.16 steps/minute; 95% CI -0.13 to 4.46; low quality of evidence), and a second meta-analysis (16 trials across Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis) reported improved comfortable walking velocity in Parkinson's disease (MD 0.21m/second, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.27) and that treadmill training had no effect on cadence. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9579750/ · keywords: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
- [statement] Reports on vitamin D supplementation and motor outcomes in Parkinson disease are mixed: a double-blind placebo-controlled trial (114 patients; vitamin D3 1200 IU/d for 12 months; Am J Clin Nutr 2013) reported that vitamin D3 significantly prevented deterioration of the Hoehn and Yahr stage (P = 0.005), a 2025 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (646 cases) found no reduction in UPDRS part III but a benefit on 6-Minute walking test distance, and a 2026 randomized trial (2000 IU/d for 12 weeks) reported no significant improvement in motor function; a 2026 review judged that firm conclusions on the disease-modifying potential of vitamin D cannot yet be drawn. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23485413/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017), section 1.6 on pharmacological neuroprotective therapy, recommends against using vitamin E as a neuroprotective therapy for people with Parkinson's disease (1.6.1) and against using co-enzyme Q10 as a neuroprotective therapy except in the context of clinical trials (1.6.2), both marked as 2006, amended 2017; a 2026 review reports that CoQ10 is classified as non-efficacious for delaying progression of PD by both the International Parkinson & Movement Disorders Society and the National Institute for Health Care Excellence at the time of writing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommends in 1.7.13 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised to take a vitamin D supplement, in 1.7.14 that creatine supplements not be offered to people with Parkinson's disease, and in 1.7.15 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised not to take over-the-counter dietary supplements without first consulting their pharmacist or other healthcare professional; a 2026 review distinguishes supplements used to correct deficiencies, such as vitamin D for bone health, which it places outside its scope, from supplements explored for disease-modifying potential. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations
- [statement] The American Academy of Neurology practice parameter on neuroprotective strategies and alternative therapies for Parkinson disease (Neurology 2006) reported the conclusions that no treatment has been shown to be neuroprotective and that there is no evidence that vitamin or food additives can improve motor function in PD; a 2026 review states that multiple phase II and III trials of pharmacological agents aimed at modulating PD pathophysiological hallmarks all failed to demonstrate significant disease-modifying effects. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16606908/
- [statement] For candidates with substantial concern about cognitive decline or depression, the CNS guideline advises considering GPi over STN while weighing the other goals of surgery; this is risk-based selection, not a guarantee of cognitive or mood safety. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/
- [statement] In the 36-month randomized-trial follow-up, quality-of-life gains diminished and cognitive measures declined despite maintained motor improvement; sustained motor benefit should not be equated with arresting disease progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385495/
- [statement] MDS-UPDRS assesses four domains: Part I non-motor experiences of daily living, Part II motor experiences of daily living, Part III motor examination, and Part IV motor complications; it is used in clinical care and research. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19025984/ · keywords: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
- [statement] The MDS website describes the MDS-UPDRS as a revision of the original Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (developed in the 1980s) that addresses problematic areas of the original scale identified by an MDS review task force; it was developed to evaluate non-motor and motor experiences of daily living and motor complications, includes a motor evaluation, and can be used in clinical settings and in research. (low confidence) — https://www.movementdisorders.org/MDS/MDS-Rating-Scales/MDS-Unified-Parkinsons-Disease-Rating-Scale-MDS-UPDRS.htm · keywords: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
- [statement] MDS red flags have explicit timing and severity: wheelchair-requiring gait progression within five years, severe autonomic failure within five years, and recurrent balance-related falls within three years; bilateral symmetric onset is another red flag. Confounding explanations and timing must be considered. (low confidence) — https://www.med.upenn.edu/digitalneuropathologylab/assets/user-content/documents/educational-resources/mds-clinical-diagnostic-criteria-for-parkinson's-disease.pdf · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] A 2024 Mayo Clinic retrospective study matched 186 women and 186 men with iRBD; 48 patients (12.9%) phenoconverted during median follow-up of 6.0 years. Only age at diagnosis remained associated with conversion in the adjusted model (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.06–1.13); the unadjusted association with antidepressant use must not be interpreted as evidence of neuroprotection. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11515114/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] A 2019 meta-analysis of seven prospective studies reported an association between hyposmia and subsequent PD, with pooled relative risk 3.84 (95% CI 2.12–6.95) across follow-up periods of 3–17 years. This relative risk is not an absolute probability that a person with hyposmia will develop PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6545790/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] NICE recommendations tagged 2017 advise against vitamin E as neuroprotective treatment, restrict co-enzyme Q10 neuroprotective use to clinical trials, and advise against creatine supplements in Parkinson disease; these adjunct supplements should not be presented as established neuroprotective therapy. (low confidence) (verified as of 2017-07-19) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
- [statement] Dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS) involves compulsive use of dopamine replacement medication beyond motor requirements, with drug seeking or hoarding, social impairment and sometimes mood elevation; distress can emerge when doses are reduced. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1736875/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] NICE recommends specialist cognitive behavioural therapy directed at ICDs when changing dopaminergic treatment is ineffective. A small randomized waiting-list-controlled trial supports short-term improvement in patient symptom severity. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] A clinical review states that non-pharmacological approaches such as limiting access to credit cards, the Internet or gambling venues should be implemented but are usually not enough on their own; a management table notes that carer involvement in surveillance can facilitate earlier detection of ICDs and that caregivers or family may participate in management when symptoms persist. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] In Parkinson’s disease, clinically important impulse control disorders include compulsive gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating; these behaviours can cause serious financial and psychosocial harm. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] NICE NG71 states that when dopamine agonist therapy is started, people and, as appropriate, their family members and carers should be given oral and written information about the increased risk of impulse control disorders, which may be concealed by the person affected, and that the discussion should be recorded; a clinical review states that all patients with PD should be advised about the potential risk of behavioural addictions, especially following dopamine agonist therapy. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] NICE NG71 states that, if a person with Parkinson's disease has developed a problematic impulse control disorder, advice should be sought from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying dopaminergic therapy, and describes first gradually reducing the dopamine agonist while monitoring both ICD response and withdrawal; a management review tabulates reducing the oral dopamine agonist while observing for resolution of ICDs, loss of motor control and dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] Previous impulsive or addictive behaviour, alcohol or smoking history, and younger age are described as risk factors for ICDs in Parkinson's disease; these are risk associations rather than diagnostic rules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] The US ONGENTYS label recommends opicapone 50 mg once daily at bedtime, without food for one hour before and at least one hour after; moderate hepatic impairment reduces the dose to 25 mg, and severe hepatic impairment calls for avoiding use. (low confidence) — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=a511a531-112e-43f8-a43f-5334b0efe979&type=display · keywords: MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
- [statement] The pharmacy review reports that high-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption and suggests coordinating meal delivery with medication times when feasible. - [statement] NICE NG71 states that people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication, and adjusted by, or only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease; a pharmacy-informatics review describes electronic order entry that can mistranscribe a patient's specific medication times and intervals. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety
- [statement] NICE advises that hospital or care-home medication changes should be made by, or discussed with, a Parkinson specialist, and that appropriate dose timing may sometimes require self-medication. - [statement] The Parkinson Foundation advises updating a written medication form whenever the routine changes and keeping a supply of current medicines in labeled pharmacy bottles for hospital use. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/hospital-safety-guide · keywords: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety
- [statement] The DLB Consortium defines dementia interfering with normal social, occupational or daily functioning as essential for DLB diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5496518/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The DLB Consortium reports that trial meta-analyses support cholinesterase inhibitors for improving cognition, global function and activities of living in DLB. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5496518/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The 2020 review recommends slow position changes, avoiding heat and large carbohydrate-rich meals, and stepwise nonpharmacological treatment; water and salt supplementation require caution in heart, kidney or liver failure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/
- [statement] Non-drug orthostatic measures include standing slowly, avoiding heat and large carbohydrate-rich meals, and individualized water and salt intake. Supplementation requires caution with heart, kidney or liver failure; abdominal binders have better supporting evidence than compression stockings in the cited review. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/
- [statement] The 2017 NICE PD recommendations advise considering midodrine with monitoring for supine hypertension, followed by consideration of fludrocortisone when midodrine is contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated; cardiac risks and interactions matter. The OH review also warns of heart or kidney failure and hypokalemia with fludrocortisone. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] The cited sources state that midodrine can be considered for PD-related OH, with attention to contraindications and supine hypertension; they describe supine and home blood-pressure monitoring as helping to balance upright benefit against hypertension while lying down. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] The cited sources state that orthostatic hypotension in PD should prompt review of blood-pressure-lowering medicines and correction of reversible contributors such as dehydration, and that it should not automatically be attributed solely to neurodegeneration. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/
- [statement] The German guideline publication in 2024 advises considering competing causes of cognitive impairment, including vitamin deficiencies and metabolic disorders, and reviewing medications with anticholinergic cognitive effects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] Memantine recommendations differ: NICE NG71 (2017) allows consideration only when cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated or not tolerated, whereas the 2024 German guideline recommends against memantine for PD dementia. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] The cited sources distinguish PD-MCI, where functional independence is preserved despite possible subtle difficulty with complex tasks, from Parkinson’s disease dementia, where cognitive impairment interferes with daily activities; motor disability alone does not establish dementia. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8073727/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] NICE NG71 (2017) recommends offering a cholinesterase inhibitor for mild or moderate Parkinson’s disease dementia and considering one for severe dementia; the severe-dementia recommendation has weaker wording. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] Cognitive training has mixed evidence: the German guideline supports it for PD-MCI but notes small, heterogeneous trials; an eight-week computerized-training RCT in PD patients with subjective cognitive complaints found no benefit on primary planning accuracy and no group differences at follow-up. The populations and interventions differ, so this is a limitation on generalization rather than proof that every training program fails. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] The 2024 German guideline says cognitive training can be offered for PD-MCI and cognitive stimulation can be offered for PD dementia; these are distinct interventions tailored to different levels of cognitive impairment. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] The 2024 German guideline recommends aerobic training for PD-MCI, while explaining that the suggested schedule is based on expert consensus and the optimal intensity and frequency have not been established. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] Cognitive training should not be presented as proven durable prevention: a PD-MCI trial reported memory benefit at six months but not twelve, while a separate broader PD trial found no cognitive advantage or difference in conversion of cognitive status at one or two years. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8563628/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] The 2024 German guideline advises against using food supplements or herbal therapeutics to treat cognitive deficits in PD-MCI or PD dementia. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] A 2021 clinical review recommends evaluating reversible contributors before attributing all cognitive change to PD, including anticholinergic drugs, benzodiazepines, opioids, and metabolic or nutritional contributors assessed through appropriate laboratory testing. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8073727/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] For PDD, the German guideline says cognitive stimulation can be offered and reminiscence therapy might be offered; it distinguishes these approaches from targeted cognitive training for PD-MCI. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] NICE advises considering augmentative and alternative communication equipment as Parkinson’s disease progresses and communication needs change. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] The dysphagia consensus recommends instrumental assessment to guide treatment; the management review recommends video fluoroscopy or video endoscopy in severe PD to adjust food and liquid consistency. (medium confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022510X21027040 · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] CBT is a supported option for anxiety in PD, but outcomes depend on the scale: the 2021 randomized trial improved the Parkinson Anxiety Scale relative to monitoring while the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale difference was not significant. The 2024 German guideline recommends offering CBT for anxiety. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/
- [statement] NICE NG71 recommends asking about hallucinations and delusions at reviews and after medication changes, and evaluating and treating medical conditions that could trigger them. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] Clozapine is an evidence-supported option for PD psychosis: the 2019 MDS review rates it clinically useful with specialized monitoring, while NICE recommends it when standard treatment is ineffective. These are evidence and guideline statements, not a claim about current monitoring regulations. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/
- [statement] NICE NG71 recommends leaving well-tolerated hallucinations and delusions untreated; potentially triggering Parkinson medicines should be reduced only with specialist advice and consideration of symptom severity and withdrawal effects. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] CBT has supportive evidence for PD depression: the 2019 MDS review rated it likely efficacious and possibly useful, while a 2024 meta-analysis found reductions in depression and anxiety; blinding constraints and the need for longer follow-up qualify confidence. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/
- [statement] CBT is supported for depressive symptoms in PD. The 2019 MDS review rated it likely efficacious and possibly useful while noting blinding and adverse-event-reporting limitations; the 2024 German guideline recommends offering CBT. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends regular exercise, frequent breaks and occupational-therapy advice for energy conservation when managing fatigue. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/fatigue · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] CBT-I is a preferred behavioral approach to insomnia, but PD-specific efficacy and implementation should be described cautiously: the computerized ACCORD-PD trial showed better insomnia scores among completers, yet its intention-to-treat comparison was not significant and treatment dropout was high. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7111581/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] Modafinil is a conditional clinical option rather than a reliably effective treatment for every sleepy PD patient: NICE says to consider it after excluding reversible causes, but a placebo-controlled trial of 40 patients found no significant improvement in subjective Epworth sleepiness or objective multiple sleep latency testing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The 2020 PD insomnia review places CBT-I within the general first-line approach to insomnia while emphasizing that PD-specific randomized trials were small; general insomnia evidence should not be presented as large-trial PD-specific proof. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7111581/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] NICE advises people with PD who have daytime sleepiness or sudden sleep onset not to drive and to consider occupational hazards; medication adjustment should follow specialist advice. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The EMA Parkinson’s guideline describes improvement of the core symptoms, motor symptoms and activities of daily living, as the endpoint for adjunctive treatment in patients on L-Dopa+ with insufficient control of motor symptoms. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease_en.pdf-0

## Parkinson's disease non-motor symptoms: neuropsychiatric symptoms, sleep disorders, autonomic dysfunction, pain and fatigue, cognitive impairment, swallowing and speech
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-non-motor-symptoms-neuropsychiatric-symptoms-sleep-disorders-autonomic-dysfunction-pain-and-fatigue-cognitive-impairment-swallowing-and-speech"></a>

- [statement] In Kubota et al.
