(Movement Disorders, first published 07 August 2026), a phase II randomized, placebo-controlled trial of an oral cannabis oil in PD patients with chronic pain (final daily dosage 43.88 mg CBD and 0.96 mg THC over 9 weeks; 101 randomized, 87 completed), the authors report no significant difference between CBD/THC and placebo in PD-PCS scores (P = 0.757) or in other non-motor scales, and the study was stopped due to futility after a pre-planned interim analysis; the authors conclude that the cannabis oil formulation did not improve pain or other non-motor symptoms compared with placebo. (low confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449 · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
- [statement] The urogenital review recommends history, bladder diary, urinalysis and post-void residual assessment, with further testing guided by findings to identify coexisting urological disease rather than attributing all urinary symptoms to PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039223/
- [statement] PD-associated pain has heterogeneous syndromes, including musculoskeletal, dystonic, peripheral/radicular and central pain; describing the pain mechanism matters before choosing treatment. (medium confidence) — https://www.mdpi.com/2035-8377/12/3/14 · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation identifies convergence insufficiency as one cause of double vision and reduced blinking with dry eyes as one cause of blurry vision in PD. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] A neuropathy review describes multiple potential contributors in people with PD, including genetic disorders, treatment effects and concomitant disease; its diagnostic approach includes history, clinical examination, blood tests and nerve-conduction studies. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7847250/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] PD fatigue is a subjective lack of energy that interferes with function; it differs from sleepiness and from objectively measured muscle fatigability. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4883681/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] A review of Parkinson-related peripheral neuropathy lists diabetes, thyroid disease and B12 deficiency among acquired causes; sensory complaints therefore warrant assessment for peripheral neuropathy rather than automatic attribution to central PD pathology. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7847250/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Rotigotine showed numerical pain improvement in an exploratory placebo-controlled pilot, but the primary pain comparison was not statistically significant; MDS classified its PD pain use as investigational rather than established efficacy. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26626320/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] The 2020 pain review distinguishes musculoskeletal, dystonic, nerve, primary and akathitic pain in PD; the heterogeneous pain presentation supports syndrome-specific assessment rather than a single analgesic strategy. (low confidence) — https://www.mdpi.com/2035-8377/12/3/14 · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Sensory symptoms in PD extend beyond pain: a 2023 review describes disturbances of vision, hearing, smell, taste, touch, temperature and position sense. This review-level observation does not establish a specific treatment for each disturbance. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37258441/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] For fatigue, the 2019 MDS review classified methylphenidate and modafinil as investigational with insufficient evidence; the Foundation likewise notes that the small positive methylphenidate trial needs further study. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] The 2020 review describes musculoskeletal pain associated with postural changes and muscular rigidity, including frozen shoulder, low back pain, arthritis and osteoporosis. (low confidence) — https://www.mdpi.com/2035-8377/12/3/14 · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] In the 2015 PANDA trial, prolonged-release oxycodone-naloxone did not meet the primary pain endpoint in the full analysis population at week 16; the authors nevertheless considered the signal worthy of further research. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26494524/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] A 2025 review of forty-one studies identified the impact of motor symptoms on daily activities and severity of neuropsychiatric symptoms as burden predictors, but found evidence inconclusive for disease stage, duration and motor symptom severity; stage or duration alone should therefore not be used as a universal burden rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Poorer caregiver mental health and greater patient neuropsychiatric symptom severity are associated with greater burden. The 2025 predictor review also identified the impact of motor symptoms on daily living, rather than motor symptoms alone, as a consistent predictor. These observational findings do not establish causality. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] In an observational analysis of 1205 participants, higher MIND and Mediterranean scores were associated with fewer patient-reported PD symptoms after adjustment for age, gender, income and years since diagnosis. This was an association with symptom scores, rather than a randomized demonstration of slowed progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/
- [statement] PD falls have multiple contributors: postural instability and gait dysfunction, including freezing, matter, and orthostatic hypotension can cause dizziness, syncope or unexplained falls. A fall assessment should therefore consider blood-pressure-related causes as well as mobility. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7220277/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Neurofilament light chain can be measured in CSF and plasma as a marker of axonal damage; higher levels have been associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in Parkinson disease, but it is nonspecific and also rises with age and other inflammatory or degenerative conditions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11226684/
- [statement] Asymmetric parkinsonism with higher cortical features such as apraxia, cortical sensory loss or alien-limb phenomena suggests corticobasal syndrome rather than typical PD. (low confidence) — https://exonpublications.com/index.php/exon/article/view/191/349 · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Essential tremor commonly produces bilateral postural/action tremor; PD can also have postural/action tremor, so tremor appearance alone is insufficient for diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://exonpublications.com/index.php/exon/article/view/191/349 · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Early prominent autonomic problems, cerebellar signs or stridor raise suspicion of multiple system atrophy; early falls with vertical eye-movement abnormalities raise suspicion of progressive supranuclear palsy. These are differential clues, not guarantees of pathology. (medium confidence) — https://exonpublications.com/index.php/exon/article/view/191/349 · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Isolated RBD involves dream enactment and loss of normal REM sleep atonia in the absence of an established neurodegenerative disorder. The cited risk cohorts used polysomnography-confirmed RBD; their estimates should not be assigned to questionnaire-positive dream enactment alone. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] Postuma and colleagues’ 2019 study followed 1280 polysomnography-confirmed iRBD patients from 24 centres: mean age was 66.3 years, 82.5% were men, and mean follow-up was 4.6 years. Overall conversion to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with Kaplan–Meier estimated conversion of 73.5% at 12 years; these are study estimates rather than universal individual prognoses. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] Smell loss alone has limited specificity: it can occur in neurological diseases other than PD. The hyposmia meta-analysis explicitly cautioned that the limited evidence did not establish hyposmia as a solid stand-alone predictor of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6545790/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] The MDS MSA criteria paper describes a clinical presentation combining autonomic failure, parkinsonism and cerebellar syndrome in varying combinations. (medium confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.29005 · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] NINDS lists trouble looking up or down among the eye and vision symptoms of PSP. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/progressive-supranuclear-palsy · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] NINDS describes Lewy body dementia as including dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson’s disease dementia. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/lewy-body-dementia · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The diagnostic-criteria review lists fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism as core clinical features of DLB. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6987529/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The Movement Disorder Society task-force abstract characterizes Parkinson’s disease dementia by impairment in attention, memory, executive and visuospatial functions. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17542011/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] NINDS states that not all people with Parkinson’s disease develop dementia and that predicting who will remains difficult. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/lewy-body-dementia · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] NINDS describes Parkinson’s disease as a progressive nervous-system disorder involving nerve-cell damage and death; WHO also describes worsening over time. (medium confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/parkinsons-disease · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] WHO and NINDS describe non-motor involvement in Parkinson’s disease, including mental-health and sleep problems. (medium confidence) — https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/parkinson-disease · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] NINDS notes that some people with Parkinson’s disease never develop tremor. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/parkinsons-disease · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] PD constipation can combine slow intestinal transit with outlet obstruction caused by impaired sphincter or puborectalis coordination; assessment should distinguish these mechanisms rather than treating every case as infrequent bowel movements alone. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5856748/
- [statement] The cited sources note that antimuscarinic bladder treatments can worsen constipation, a trade-off relevant to urinary urgency in a person with PD who already has bowel symptoms. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039223/
- [statement] Rivastigmine’s cognitive benefit must be balanced against tolerability: its dementia trial found more nausea, vomiting and tremor than placebo, and the German guideline also recognizes tremor and worsening PD symptoms as adverse effects. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15590953/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] PD-related swallowing impairment can cause aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition and dehydration; assessment and rehabilitation therefore address safety and nutrition as well as symptoms. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2784698/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] PD dysarthria can involve reduced volume, monotone pitch, imprecise articulation, altered voice quality and irregular rhythm; it is described as a motor feature even when included in a broader non-motor symptom review. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] The sialorrhea review attributes PD drooling mainly to impaired saliva clearance and reduced swallowing rather than increased saliva production; cited sialometry studies found reduced production relative to people without PD. (low confidence) — https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6651/12/11/691 · keywords: PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends recording fatigue timing and its relationship to medication, evaluating non-PD causes such as anemia, pacing activity with breaks, regular exercise, and occupational-therapy advice on energy conservation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/fatigue · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Sensory symptoms include diminished smell, which can precede PD diagnosis; the Parkinson’s Foundation notes that reduced smell can also reduce enjoyment of food and appetite. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/non-movement-symptoms · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] Polysomnography is not routine for uncomplicated insomnia assessment, but can help when sleep-disordered breathing, RBD or other sleep-related movements may explain disturbed sleep. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7111581/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] NICE recommends considering modafinil for PD-related excessive daytime sleepiness only after a detailed sleep history excludes reversible drug-related and physical causes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The cited review describes insomnia assessment as including a clinical sleep interview that checks medication effects, the sleep environment and comorbid sleep disorders; it notes that polysomnography is not routine for insomnia but may help when sleep-disordered breathing, RBD or other nocturnal movements are suspected. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7111581/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] NICE advises that PD patients with daytime sleepiness or sudden sleep onset avoid driving and consider occupational hazards, with specialist-guided medication adjustment. It advises considering modafinil only after a detailed sleep history excludes reversible medication-related and physical causes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] PD sleep complaints require separate assessment of insomnia, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and excessive daytime sleepiness; results on overall sleep quality should not be assumed to establish efficacy for each phenotype. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13612690/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] RBD involves loss of REM muscle atonia with dream enactment and potential injury; a 2021 critical review describes clinical dream-enactment history plus video-polysomnographic confirmation as necessary for diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8739295/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] For PD patients with obstructive sleep apnea, the 2019 MDS review considered CPAP likely efficacious and possibly useful for improving sleep and daytime sleepiness; this evidence does not apply indiscriminately to all PD sleepiness. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] RBD involves loss of normal REM muscle atonia and dream enactment that can injure the patient or bed partner. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071384/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] Foltynie and colleagues describe MDS UPDRS Part 1 as capturing non-motor symptoms, Part 2 as capturing motor impact on daily living, Part 3 as clinician-assessed motor severity, and Part 4 as motor complications. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13438061/

## Parkinson's disease neurobiology and disease landscape: dopamine circuits, alpha-synuclein spread, neurodegeneration mechanisms, atypical parkinsonism, Lewy body dementia and age, sex and ancestry differences
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-neurobiology-and-landscape-dopamine-circuits-alpha-synuclein-spread-atypical-parkinsonism-lewy-body-dementia-and-subgroups"></a>

- [statement] NINDS states that a dopamine transporter scan cannot distinguish Parkinson’s disease from atypical parkinsonism; Beach and Adler likewise describe dopamine functional scans as lacking specificity for Parkinson’s disease. (medium confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/parkinsons-disease · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] In the US Medicare study, age-standardized Parkinson disease incidence and prevalence were greater in men than women across the racial groups studied; the Parkinson’s Foundation also reports higher incidence estimates in men. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2865395/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society task force defines early-onset Parkinson’s disease as onset after 21 years but before 50 years. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The task-force review reports that genetic predisposition may be more likely with younger age at Parkinson’s disease onset. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The task-force review reports that most studies find slower motor-symptom progression in early-onset than late-onset Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The task-force review describes unemployment in early-onset Parkinson’s disease as a burden that can include social isolation and loss of purpose and self-esteem. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The US Medicare study reports lower mean age-standardized Parkinson disease prevalence among Black and Asian beneficiaries than among White beneficiaries in its historical study population. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2865395/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] In the Korean genome-wide association study, the authors report the strongest Parkinson’s disease associations at the SNCA and PARK16 loci. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-023-00580-3 · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The Korean study’s authors identify limited statistical power, particularly after sex stratification, as a limitation of their genetic association results. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-023-00580-3 · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The FENS release states that a limitation of the presented study is the small number of samples investigated. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://www.fens.org/news-activities/news/why-does-parkinsons-disease-affect-more-men-than-women-study-reveals-differences-in-gene-activity-in-the-brain · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] Sources differ on the sex gradient in Asian populations: the US Medicare study reports greater age-standardized prevalence and incidence in men than in women for all races studied, whereas Park and colleagues state that Parkinson's disease is more prevalent in women in Asian populations, including the Korean population. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2865395/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The review states that the GBA variants 84insGG and R496H increase risk of PD exclusively in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. (low confidence) — https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3233/JPD-191763 · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society task force review states that the most frequent genetic mutations associated with EOPD are located on parkin (PARK2), PINK1 (PARK 6), the PARK7 gene, ATP13A2 (PARK9) and PLA2G6 (PARK14). (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The task force recommends the term early-onset Parkinson’s disease rather than young-onset Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The task-force review reports that levodopa-induced dyskinesia is more frequent with younger age at onset. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9547138/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The epidemiology review cautions that self-declared race or ethnicity has been used as a surrogate for genetic ancestry despite reflecting sociocultural conditions more closely. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11123577/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] In the Korean study’s male-only analysis, no single nucleotide polymorphism surpassed the genome-wide significance threshold after Bonferroni correction. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-023-00580-3 · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] Schaffner and colleagues report more associations of blood DNAm with PD in females (69 regions) than in males (2 regions) in a region-based analysis of agricultural workers (71 early-stage PD cases, 147 controls). (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11076573/ · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] In the FENS release, the presenting investigator reports that, across five brain regions, PD caused common changes regardless of sex, together with differences between men and women in gene activity in some cells and some brain regions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://www.fens.org/news-activities/news/why-does-parkinsons-disease-affect-more-men-than-women-study-reveals-differences-in-gene-activity-in-the-brain · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] The FENS release reports that mitochondria-linked gene activity differed between sexes in astrocytes and that myelin-related gene activity differed between sexes in oligodendrocytes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://www.fens.org/news-activities/news/why-does-parkinsons-disease-affect-more-men-than-women-study-reveals-differences-in-gene-activity-in-the-brain · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] In the brain-first versus body-first model, brain-first Parkinson's disease has α-synuclein pathology initially arising in the brain and spreading to the peripheral autonomic nervous system, while body-first Parkinson's disease has pathology originating in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system and then spreading to the brain. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/
- [statement] In a preprint of an autopsy study of 50 PD subjects, the authors report that a positive SAA or IHC result was restricted to the GI tract in only 2 subjects while Lewy body pathology by either SAA or IHC was restricted to the brain in 11 subjects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13042094/
- [statement] Mutations in the Parkin and PINK1 proteins are the most common form of autosomal recessive PD. (high confidence) — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.ady0240 · keywords: Mitochondrial and mitophagy targets: PINK1, parkin, USP30
- [statement] SAA seeding activity and total CSF alpha-synuclein concentration are different measurements: the 2024 Zarkali review found that total CSF alpha-synuclein did not show a consistent relationship with Lewy body pathology or longitudinal motor or cognitive change. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11226684/
- [statement] Pathogenic SNCA variants cause rare autosomal dominant PD; point mutations and gene multiplications are relevant variant classes. SNCA penetrance and phenotype depend on the variant. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10946878/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] Large studies have not demonstrated increased PD risk from a single heterozygous pathogenic PRKN variant. The UK Biobank/NIH-PD study found similar PD likelihood in single-variant carriers and noncarriers; this does not establish recessive PRKN disease in a monoallelic carrier. (medium confidence) — https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/publications/heterozygous-prkn-mutations-are-common-but-do-not-increase-the-risk-of-parkinsons-disease/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] A meta-analysis of 17 datasets from Parkinson's disease genome-wide association studies in European ancestry samples identified 90 independent genome-wide significant risk signals across 78 genomic regions; these 90 variants explained 16-36% of the heritable risk of Parkinson's disease depending on prevalence. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31701892/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] Examples of 2015 MDS absolute exclusions are unequivocal cerebellar abnormalities, downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy or selective slowing of downward saccades, and dopamine-blocking/depleting exposure whose dose and time course fit drug-induced parkinsonism. (low confidence) — https://www.med.upenn.edu/digitalneuropathologylab/assets/user-content/documents/educational-resources/mds-clinical-diagnostic-criteria-for-parkinson's-disease.pdf · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] The Braak pathological sequence is not universal across patients or Lewy-body disorders; reviews describe nonconforming distributions, so it should not be assumed to represent every patient’s disease course. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] In the same 2019 iRBD cohort, olfactory deficit predicted faster phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 2.62), alongside quantitative motor abnormalities (3.16) and mild cognitive impairment (1.91–2.37); the outcome was overall neurodegenerative phenoconversion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] The strain review proposes that cellular environments encountered during propagation may influence alpha-synuclein aggregate structure and function; this is presented as a hypothesis. (low confidence) — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/aging-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnagi.2022.907293/full · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] A PubMed abstract states the hypothesis that Parkinson's disease comprises a brain-first type, with alpha-synuclein pathology arising in the brain and secondarily spreading to the peripheral autonomic nervous system, and a body-first type, with pathology originating in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system and then spreading to the brain. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] The reviews describe alpha-synuclein as a protein concentrated at presynaptic nerve terminals. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8347623/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] The aggregation review describes an amphipathic amino-terminal region of alpha-synuclein with an important lipid-binding role. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8347623/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] Luk and colleagues report that intrastriatal synthetic alpha-synuclein fibril inoculation in wildtype non-transgenic mice produced Lewy-like pathology in anatomically interconnected regions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552321/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] In the inoculated mouse model, Luk and colleagues report progressive dopamine-neuron loss in the substantia nigra pars compacta accompanying Lewy pathology accumulation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552321/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] Brundin and Melki propose neuron-to-neuron transfer as essential for regional Lewy pathology spread; Surmeier and colleagues argue that the spreading hypothesis is difficult to reconcile with human postmortem and connectome evidence. (low confidence) — https://www.jneurosci.org/content/37/41/9808 · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] Spillantini and colleagues report that Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites contain abnormal filamentous alpha-synuclein material. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18591134/ · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Spillantini and colleagues classify Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy as alpha-synucleinopathies; Shahnawaz and colleagues likewise group them as diseases associated with α-synuclein misfolding and aggregation. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18591134/ · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Schweighauser and colleagues report that MSA brain-extracted α-synuclein filament structures differ from structures formed in vitro using recombinant proteins. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2317-6 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Yang and colleagues describe MSA α-synuclein inclusions as especially prominent in oligodendrocytes, consistent with the glial cytoplasmic inclusions described by Spillantini and colleagues. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05319-3 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Lee and colleagues describe neuronal soma Lewy bodies and axonal or dendritic Lewy neurites in PD, PDD and DLB. (low confidence) — https://elifesciences.org/articles/92775 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Yang and colleagues report a single-protofilament Lewy fold in α-synuclein filaments extracted from the brains of individuals with PD, PDD and DLB. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05319-3 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Alexander and colleagues describe CBD neuropathology as aggregated 4-repeat tau protein isoforms deposited in neurons and glial cells. (low confidence) — https://jnnp.bmj.com/content/85/8/925 · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] Alexander and colleagues distinguish corticobasal syndrome from CBD pathology: patients with similar corticobasal syndromes can have other neurodegenerative pathologies. (low confidence) — https://jnnp.bmj.com/content/85/8/925 · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] The nigrostriatal axonal projection carries the influence of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons to the striatum, as described by the axonal review and the circuit review. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-13) — https://www.dovepress.com/degeneration-of-nigrostriatal-dopaminergic-axons-in-parkinsons-disease-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-NDT · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] Rocha and colleagues describe the striatum as the main input hub within the interconnected basal ganglia nuclei. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] Cui and colleagues contrast the classical opposing-pathways model with their mouse observation of increased activity in both pathways at action initiation. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4039389/ · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] The nigrostriatal axonal review states that the temporal sequence and causal relationship between early axonal functional abnormalities and structural degeneration remain unclear. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-13) — https://www.dovepress.com/degeneration-of-nigrostriatal-dopaminergic-axons-in-parkinsons-disease-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-NDT · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] The Movement Disorder Society task-force abstract identifies Lewy body-type degeneration in cerebral cortex and limbic structures as the main pathological correlate of Parkinson’s disease dementia. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17542011/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The DLB Consortium notes that abundant neocortical neuritic plaques and tangles accompanying Lewy bodies can produce a clinical profile resembling Alzheimer disease rather than typical DLB. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5496518/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The DLB Consortium states that normal dopamine-transporter uptake can occur in autopsy-confirmed DLB. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5496518/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] In dopaminergic neurons derived from patients with idiopathic and familial Parkinson’s disease, Burbulla and colleagues report a cascade linking mitochondrial oxidant stress through oxidized dopamine accumulation to reduced glucocerebrosidase activity and lysosomal dysfunction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6021018/
- [statement] Burbulla and colleagues report that the toxic cascade was observed in human but not mouse Parkinson’s disease neurons, partly because of species-specific dopamine metabolism. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6021018/
- [statement] Brochard and colleagues report brain infiltration by CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, but not B cells, in postmortem human Parkinson disease specimens and in the MPTP mouse model during neuronal degeneration. (low confidence) — https://www.jci.org/articles/view/36470
- [statement] The ethnic-variation narrative review states that LRRK2 p.G2019S is the most common genetic cause of PD worldwide, accounting for 1% of sporadic PD and 4% of familial PD. (low confidence) — https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3233/JPD-191763 · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD
- [statement] A FENS press release states that research presented at the FENS Forum 2026 compared post-mortem brain samples from 73 people with PD (28 women and 45 men) with 24 controls (9 women and 15 men). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://www.fens.org/news-activities/news/why-does-parkinsons-disease-affect-more-men-than-women-study-reveals-differences-in-gene-activity-in-the-brain · keywords: Sex, age and ancestry differences and young-onset PD

## Parkinson's disease diagnosis and biomarkers: clinical criteria, prodromal stage, staging, genetics, alpha-synuclein seed amplification, imaging, epidemiology and rating scales
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-diagnosis-and-biomarkers-clinical-criteria-prodromal-stage-staging-genetics-alpha-synuclein-seed-amplification-imaging-epidemiology-and-rating-scales"></a>

- [statement] A blinded comparison of three independent laboratories using PPMI CSF samples reported sensitivities of 86–96% and specificities of 93–100%, demonstrating reproducibility in expert laboratories despite methodological differences. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8572469/
- [statement] The 2025 biomatrix meta-analysis reported pooled blood SAA sensitivity of 0.90 (95% CI 0.86–0.93) and specificity of 0.91 (0.86–0.95); these pooled estimates are limited by aggregate data, publication bias and heterogeneous studies, and do not establish a universal blood-test performance. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12192484/
- [statement] In an analysis of PPMI and Tübingen cohort data, baseline SAA time-to-threshold predicted cognitive decline in both PPMI (hazard ratio 2·36, 95% CI 1·60–3·46) and Tübingen (2·17, 1·07–4·41), and was associated with cognitive decline in an Alzheimer-biomarker-negative PPMI subgroup. This was an observational prognostic association. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40541208/
- [statement] The FDA’s August 19, 2024 Letter of Support recommends CSF SAA as a susceptibility/risk biomarker for trial enrichment and supports binary SAA assessment for selection into trials targeting common synuclein biology; its stated context is drug development and clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-08-19) — https://www.fda.gov/media/181368/download
- [statement] A Viewpoint cautions against premature adoption of the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay as a Parkinson disease biomarker test in general neurology practice; this is an attributed clinical-implementation caution. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39102226/
- [statement] In the 2023 cross-sectional PPMI study, CSF SAA sensitivity for clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease was 87·7% (95% CI 84·9–90·5) and specificity against healthy controls was 96·3% (93·4–99·2); these estimates describe that study population rather than general-population screening. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10627170/
- [statement] SAA positivity is heterogeneous: in the 2023 PPMI study, sensitivity in sporadic Parkinson disease with olfactory deficit was 98·6%, compared with 78·3% without olfactory deficit. A negative result therefore cannot universally exclude clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10627170/
- [statement] NfL is a marker of neuroaxonal injury that can complement alpha-synuclein SAA, rather than directly measuring alpha-synuclein seeds. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12037818/
- [statement] The 2024 Zarkali review reports associations of baseline CSF Alzheimer-related biomarkers—higher phosphorylated tau, lower amyloid-beta 42, and lower amyloid-beta 42/total tau ratio—with worsening motor and cognitive performance at follow-up; these characterize co-pathology and prognosis rather than alpha-synuclein seeding itself. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11226684/
- [statement] In a blinded 30-site cross-sectional study, skin biopsy detected cutaneous phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in 92.7% (89 of 96) of patients with PD, 98.2% (54 of 55) with MSA, 96.0% (48 of 50) with DLB and 100% (22 of 22) with pure autonomic failure, versus 3.3% (4 of 120) of controls; the authors state that further research in unselected clinical populations is needed to externally validate the findings. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10955354/
- [statement] Alpha-synuclein SAA detects seeding-competent misfolded aggregates by amplifying their ability to template recombinant alpha-synuclein aggregation; thioflavin T fluorescence detects the resulting fibrils. RT-QuIC and PMCA are related SAA approaches. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8572469/
- [statement] Expert-laboratory concordance does not remove the need for assay standardization: protocol heterogeneity, recombinant substrate, buffers, beads, shaking, temperature, and preanalytical handling affect comparability. (high confidence) — https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/acn3.70384
- [statement] Blood alpha-synuclein assays require control of peripheral contamination and sample handling: erythrocytes and platelets contribute alpha-synuclein, and hemolysis and storage conditions can vary results. CSF SAA also requires preanalytical controls, including blood contamination and freeze-thaw handling. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12192484/
- [statement] Longitudinal prognostic results differ by analysis: a PPMI analysis found no statistically significant association between baseline seeding measures and progression among manifest patients, whereas a separate analysis associated baseline time-to-threshold with subsequent cognitive decline in PPMI and an independent Tübingen cohort. Diagnostic positivity should not be treated as an established general progression measure. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12354789/
- [statement] CSF sampling is relatively invasive, motivating SAA studies in other specimens. The 2024 Zarkali review describes promising skin-biopsy results and lower accuracy with olfactory-mucosa sampling; performance should be interpreted for the specimen and assay actually tested. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11226684/
- [statement] The PDQ-39 is a short 39-item quality-of-life questionnaire for Parkinson's disease whose data can be presented in profile form or as a single index; a briefer derived measure (PDQ-8) also exists. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9617716/ · keywords: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
- [statement] In the DATSCAN label's two multicenter studies of 284 adult patients with suspected parkinsonian syndromes, the clinical reference category parkinsonian syndromes (PS) comprised Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy, and the label states that DATSCAN imaging was not designed to distinguish among these conditions. (low confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/022454s010lbl.pdf · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommends considering 123I‑FP‑CIT SPECT for people with tremor if essential tremor cannot be clinically differentiated from parkinsonism, and says not to use PET in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes except in the context of clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) says not to use structural MRI to diagnose Parkinson's disease, while structural MRI may be considered in the differential diagnosis of other parkinsonian syndromes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] In the Movement Disorders systematic review of neuroimaging-based AI studies, the authors report that the majority of studies aimed to distinguish PD patients from healthy controls (54%) or atypical parkinsonian syndromes (25%), whereas prognostic or interventional studies were sparse. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] One review cites a UK autopsy study that found the misdiagnosis rate of PD is 24%, and a neuroimaging review states that the heterogeneous disease phenotype and overlapping symptoms with atypical parkinsonian syndromes (APS) contribute to high misdiagnosis rates. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] In a machine learning study of longitudinal clinical data from a Parkinson's progression cohort, the authors report projections of disease progression 5 years after initial diagnosis with an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.92 for the slower progressing group and 0.95 ± 0.02 for the fast-progressing group. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9758217/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The authors of the progression study report that they replicated their findings in an independent cohort, released the analytical code, and identified serum neurofilament light as a significant indicator of fast disease progression among other key biomarkers of interest. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9758217/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] Data leakage inflates reported accuracy in PD machine learning: the neuroimaging review reports that data leakage was associated with a significant inflation of accuracies, and a separate study reports that without overt features all models exhibited superficially acceptable F1 scores but failed catastrophically in specificity, with the authors attributing high accuracy when overt features were included to data leakage rather than genuine predictive power. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] A preprint auditing evaluation protocols reports that subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780, and that supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14533 · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The biomarker review states that its proportions describe the sample assessed, not the entire PD machine learning literature, and an earlier review likewise describes its work as sampling current ML practices in PD applications. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] In a UK Biobank analysis, the authors report that machine learning models trained on accelerometry data distinguished clinically diagnosed Parkinson's disease (n = 153) with an AUPRC of 0.14 ± 0.04, and prodromal Parkinson's disease (n = 113) up to 7 years pre-diagnosis with an AUPRC of 0.07 ± 0.03, from the general population (n = 33,009), outperforming models based on genetics, lifestyle, blood biochemistry or prodromal symptoms data. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37400639/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] A scoping review of prodromal Parkinson's disease and a systematic review of wearable sensors for early diagnosis each report that most included studies were cross-sectional. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13697243/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] Studies in different cohorts report that Parkinson's disease subtypes differ in progression: one reports clusters associated with motor progression rates, another reports faster two-year progression in diffuse-malignant patients, and a third reports that data-driven subtypes exhibited the highest progression rates. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6288789/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] The SynNeurGe classification of Parkinson's disease proposes three components, pathological α-synuclein, neurodegeneration defined by neuroimaging and pathogenic gene variants, linked to a clinical component; its authors emphasise initial application exclusively for research, and a European Academy of Neurology page lists it among two recent research frameworks for a biological definition of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] Two analyses of the PPMI cohort by different author groups report that LRRK2-associated Parkinson's disease includes cases negative on the CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay: one reports 46 negative and 102 positive among 148 LRRK2 parkinsonism cases, and another reports SAA-negative patients were markedly enriched for LRRK2 variants. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11925012/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] Reports differ on motor progression in SAA-negative Parkinson's disease: an analysis of LRRK2 carriers reports less severe motor manifestations and decline without alpha-synuclein aggregates, while a European Academy of Neurology commentary on a PPMI analysis reports faster time to motor disability milestones in SAA-negative PD, with a relatively small sample. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11925012/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] Courage-PD estimated OR 0.74 (95% CI 0.60–0.93) for PD per standard-deviation increase in genetically predicted smoking initiation. It found no significant coffee or alcohol association but cautioned that conclusions for those two exposures were limited by insufficient statistical power. MR interpretation depends on valid instrumental-variable assumptions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation interview states the ORCHESTRA trial was launched before the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay existed, so it is not known for sure that enrolled participants had the misfolded alpha-synuclein pathology the drug targeted. (low confidence) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/news/news-context-mixed-results-two-experimental-drugs-targeting-alpha-synuclein · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- [statement] The Lancet PADOVA paper describes prasinezumab as a humanised monoclonal antibody that binds the C-terminus of aggregated forms of α-synuclein. (medium confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673626008652
- [statement] The ASPro-PD protocol gives the primary outcome as the combined score of parts I, II, and III of the MDS-UPDRS, whereas the Cure Parkinson's trial page says the MDS-UPDRS Part III rating scale will be used to measure changes in motor symptoms. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12916515/ · keywords: GBA1, ambroxol and lysosomal-targeted therapies
- [statement] In the 2025 head-to-head NfL study, CSF assays discriminated Parkinson’s disease from atypical parkinsonian disorders more accurately than plasma assays (AUC 0.966–0.974 versus 0.917–0.924); combining CSF NfL with alpha-synuclein RT-QuIC improved accuracy in that cohort. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12037818/
- [statement] The MDS Non-Motor Rating Scale (MDS-NMS) consists of 13 domains plus a subscale for non-motor fluctuations and is rater-administered; in its initial multicenter validation study, internal consistency was acceptable (average Cronbach's alpha 0.66 and 0.84 for the scale total and the non-motor fluctuations total), interrater reliability was excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient >0.95) and test-retest intraclass correlation was 0.84 for the scale total. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31571279/ · keywords: Clinical rating scales and outcome measures: MDS-UPDRS
- [statement] PRKN- and PINK1-related PD have autosomal recessive inheritance and are especially relevant in early-onset disease; established recessive disease must be distinguished from finding a single heterozygous variant. (medium confidence) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1223/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] GeneReviews describes PRKN-related PD as usually beginning before age 35 with slow progression and relatively milder non-motor manifestations; PINK1-related PD has a similar phenotype, with psychiatric features more prominent. (low confidence) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1223/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] PD panels need attention to copy-number analysis: sequencing alone may miss deletions or duplications, particularly relevant to SNCA and PRKN. Check whether the assay includes deletion/duplication testing. (medium confidence) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1223/ · keywords: Genetics of PD: LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1
- [statement] Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI is an emerging candidate biomarker, but the strong performance of a small retrospective 7T study does not establish its accuracy in premotor, equivocal or atypical cases: its authors explicitly called for studies in those populations. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00631-3 · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] Conventional structural MRI identifies vascular damage, masses and patterns of atrophy that can cause or help distinguish parkinsonism; ordinary anatomical sequences have limited ability to identify the dopaminergic deficit itself. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6280219/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] A 2024 retrospective 7T neuromelanin MRI study included 21 PD patients, 13 essential-tremor patients and 18 controls; substantia nigra pars compacta total volume distinguished PD from the pooled non-PD group with reported sensitivity 100% and specificity 96.8%. These are within-study results. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00631-3 · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] Presynaptic dopamine-transporter imaging supports distinguishing essential tremor from neurodegenerative parkinsonism; an abnormal DaTscan is not specific for idiopathic Parkinson’s disease and cannot reliably separate it from atypical degenerative parkinsonism. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] Conventional structural MRI generally does not confirm PD, but can identify alternative structural causes or findings suggesting atypical parkinsonism; its sensitivity for atypical syndromes is limited early in disease. (medium confidence) — https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/what-is-a-datscan-and-should-i-get-one/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The EANM/SNMMI guideline describes fluorodopa PET as a presynaptic dopaminergic assessment and notes that atypical parkinsonian syndromes usually cannot be separated from idiopathic PD with this technique; FDG-PET instead evaluates metabolic patterns. PET tracers should therefore not be treated as interchangeable tests. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The EANM/SNMMI guideline warns that DAT binding reaches a floor later in disease, weakening its correlation with further clinical progression; scan signal should not be treated as a universally linear progression measure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The DATSCAN label (revised 11/2022) states that its effectiveness as a screening or confirmatory test, and for monitoring disease progression or response to therapy, has not been established. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/022454s010lbl.pdf · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] In the EANM/SNMMI guideline, early idiopathic Parkinson’s disease typically shows reduced uptake first in the posterior putamen opposite the symptomatic side, with greater putaminal than caudate involvement; this is a typical pattern rather than a disease-specific signature. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The EANM/SNMMI guideline interprets persistent scans without dopaminergic deficit as evidence against idiopathic PD; Palermo and colleagues instead reported eight older-onset levodopa-responsive cases with initially normal scans, two later abnormal. Their cases lacked pathological confirmation, so this is an attributed limitation rather than proof that normal scans commonly miss PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] A 2023 retrospective clinical series of 156 patients referred for suspected atypical parkinsonism found overall FDG-PET classification accuracy of 74%, using follow-up clinical diagnosis rather than autopsy as the reference; the reader had access to prior dopamine-transporter imaging. The authors acknowledge reference-standard bias and missing histopathological confirmation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10423182/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] DaTscan uses iodine-123 ioflupane SPECT to visualize striatal dopamine transporter availability; it is an adjunct to other diagnostic evaluations rather than a standalone disease identification test. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/022454s010lbl.pdf · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] For dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), the DATSCAN label reports, in 55 patients clinically diagnosed with DLB or Alzheimer's disease and compared with autopsy diagnosis, sensitivity of 80% (95% CI 61% to 92%) and specificity of 92% (95% CI 74% to 99%); the label derives this evidence from the scientific literature. (low confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/022454s010lbl.pdf · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] A meta-analysis of nigrosome-1 appearance on MRI included nineteen studies with a total of 1508 participants (903 idiopathic PD patients and 605 healthy controls) and reported pooled sensitivity 0.94 (95 percent CI 0.93-0.96) and specificity 0.90 (95 percent CI 0.88-0.92) for differentiating idiopathic PD from healthy adults; the comparison was with healthy adults rather than other parkinsonian syndromes. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668370/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] A 2014 primary MRI study showed that healthy nigrosome-1 can appear as a swallow-tail hyperintensity on high-resolution 3T susceptibility-weighted imaging, with this appearance lost in PD. The authors called for independent prospective validation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3977922/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The 2024 7T MRI authors identify small sample size, retrospective design and inclusion of established PD as limitations, and call for studies in equivocal PD and atypical parkinsonism; their reported accuracy should not be assumed to generalize to routine diagnostic populations. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00631-3 · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] In the same 7T study, neuromelanin volume discriminated groups, whereas contrast ratio did not differ significantly between PD and non-PD groups; a result for one MRI metric should not be generalized to all neuromelanin measurements. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00631-3 · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] In a retrospective study of eighty-three clinically confirmed degenerative parkinsonian cases, voxel-based FDG-PET maps added diagnostic accuracy and confidence, particularly for less experienced readers; expert-reader improvement was mainly supported by hypometabolism maps. (low confidence) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-022-06166-w · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] The 2015 MDS criteria first require motor parkinsonism: bradykinesia together with rest tremor, rigidity, or both. Parkinsonism alone does not establish PD as its cause. (medium confidence) — https://www.med.upenn.edu/digitalneuropathologylab/assets/user-content/documents/educational-resources/mds-clinical-diagnostic-criteria-for-parkinson's-disease.pdf · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] NICE NG71 recommends prompt, untreated referral to a specialist in differential diagnosis when PD is suspected, and regular diagnostic review at six- to twelve-month intervals with reconsideration if atypical features develop. Its diagnostic recommendation explicitly names the UK Brain Bank criteria. (low confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] In the 2018 eight-centre validation cohort of 626 patients, probable MDS PD had 94.5% sensitivity, 88.5% specificity and 92.6% overall accuracy against expert clinical diagnosis. These estimates measure agreement with expert clinical diagnosis, not autopsy confirmation. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30145797/ · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] The 2015 MDS criteria were designed to codify expert clinical diagnosis for research and can guide clinical assessment; diagnostic accuracy varies with disease duration and examiner expertise, so criteria performance should not be treated as one universal accuracy number. (medium confidence) — https://www.med.upenn.edu/digitalneuropathologylab/assets/user-content/documents/educational-resources/mds-clinical-diagnostic-criteria-for-parkinson's-disease.pdf · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] The UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria, reproduced from Gibb and Lees (1988), first define a parkinsonian syndrome as bradykinesia plus at least one of muscular rigidity, 4–6 Hz rest tremor, or postural instability not caused by primary visual, vestibular, cerebellar or proprioceptive dysfunction (step 1); step 2 lists exclusion criteria for Parkinson’s disease, including supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early severe autonomic involvement and neuroleptic treatment at onset of symptoms. (low confidence) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK379754/ · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Step 3 of the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank criteria lists supportive prospective positive criteria, three or more of which are required for diagnosis of definite Parkinson’s disease: unilateral onset, rest tremor present, progressive disorder, persistent asymmetry affecting the side of onset most, excellent response (70–100%) to levodopa, severe levodopa-induced chorea, levodopa response for 5 years or more, and a clinical course of 10 years or more. (low confidence) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK379754/ · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] Clinically established PD under the 2015 MDS criteria requires no absolute exclusion, at least two supportive criteria, and no red flags. Clinically probable PD permits at most two red flags, each counterbalanced by a supportive criterion, with no absolute exclusion. (medium confidence) — https://www.med.upenn.edu/digitalneuropathologylab/assets/user-content/documents/educational-resources/mds-clinical-diagnostic-criteria-for-parkinson's-disease.pdf · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] The autopsy-based scoping review by Fox and colleagues found that supportive features were more common in PD and exclusions/red flags more common in atypical disorders, but some atypical features also occurred in pathologically confirmed PD. Limited clinical documentation, retrospective application of precise definitions and co-pathology constrain interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12748991/ · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) advises against acute levodopa and apomorphine challenge tests in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes, and against objective smell testing in that setting except in the context of clinical trials. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: PD diagnosis criteria and differential diagnosis
- [statement] SynNeurGe links its biological components to a clinical component C, defined by either a single high-specificity feature or multiple lower-specificity clinical features. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] In their 2024 comparison, Höglinger and Lang classify an isolated S-positive result without confirmed neurodegeneration as Parkinson’s/Lewy-type synucleinopathy, whereas they describe NSD-ISS as assigning such individuals stage 1A; they dispute treating this finding alone as a clinical disease diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1877718X241298194 · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Burke and colleagues cautioned that Braak pathological stages cannot be directly equated with clinical severity or inevitable future clinical Parkinson’s disease: their review describes advanced pathological stages in neurologically unimpaired individuals and no relationship with clinical severity in the data examined. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] SynNeurGe’s proposed biological classification has three components: pathological α-synuclein in tissues or CSF (S), imaging evidence of neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic variants that cause or strongly predispose to Parkinson’s disease (G). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Published interpretations differ: an autopsy-based study concluded that the PD staging scheme is valid except in the setting of advanced Alzheimer’s disease, whereas Burke and colleagues judged the evidence insufficient to establish the proposed caudal-to-rostral temporal progression of human Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20187227/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] In an analysis of PPMI, PASADENA and SPARK data published in npj Parkinson's Disease in 2024, 1741 participants had SAA data and 1030 (59%) were S+ consistent with neuronal alpha-synuclein disease (NSD); among sporadic PD, 683/736 (93%) were NSD, with a baseline distribution across NSD-ISS Stages 2B, 3 and 4 of 25%, 63% and 9%. The authors state that validation of the proposed anchors in longitudinal cohorts is necessary. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-024-00789-w · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Braak staging proposes a neuropathological sequence beginning in lower-brainstem or olfactory structures, proceeding toward substantia nigra involvement and eventually cortex; the proposed direction of spread is a hypothesis rather than a clinical disability score. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Braak’s six-pattern scheme inferred temporal progression from progressively broader postmortem distributions of abnormal α-synuclein staining; in that proposed sequence substantia-nigra involvement appears around stage 3, rather than at its earliest stage. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] SynNeurGe classifies pathological α-synuclein (S), neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic genetic variants (G), linked to clinical manifestations (C); these are biological classification dimensions. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Braak and colleagues interpreted increasingly extensive, nested pathological distributions as a temporal sequence: stage 1 involved medulla or olfactory structures, stage 2 added rostrally adjacent brainstem structures, and stages 3–4 were proposed to coincide with substantia nigra neuron loss and clinical parkinsonism. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · keywords: PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- [statement] Isolated RBD is a strong prodromal marker for a spectrum of neurodegenerative outcomes, including Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy; a reported overall phenoconversion rate is therefore not a PD-only conversion rate. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] A negative baseline prodromal assessment cannot reliably rule out later phenoconversion in iRBD. In the 2019 cohort, even participants negative for the MDS prodromal criteria had conversion estimates of 5% at 3 years, 13% at 5 years and 27% at 8 years. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] The MDS research framework combines an age-based prior probability with marker likelihood ratios in a Bayesian naïve classifier; probable prodromal PD means at least 80% estimated certainty that prodromal disease is present, rather than an 80% prediction of clinical conversion within a specified number of years. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] The 2024 Lifelines analysis found poor discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.577) using a subset of MDS risk and prodromal markers in 160 self-reported PD converters and 320 matched controls. Only six of eleven risk markers and six of twelve prodromal markers could be inferred, so this result scopes a partial, largely questionnaire-based implementation rather than invalidating the complete criteria. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208573/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] Prodromal PD describes early symptoms or signs of neurodegeneration before fully evolved motor parkinsonism permits a classic clinical diagnosis; the original MDS prodromal criteria were explicitly developed for research purposes only. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] The 2019 update of the MDS prodromal framework revised marker weights using new prospective evidence; in particular, the positive likelihood ratio for olfactory loss increased, while many marker likelihood ratios were unchanged. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31412427/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
- [statement] Polymeropoulos and colleagues identified an alpha-synuclein gene mutation in families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9197268/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] The abstract of the staging study 'Staging of brain pathology related to sporadic Parkinson's disease' states that lesions initially occur in the dorsal motor nucleus of the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves and the anterior olfactory nucleus, and proposes a staging procedure based on the topographical extent of the lesions. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12498954/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] In the PET case-control study described in that abstract (37 de novo Parkinson's disease patients: 24 RBD-negative and 13 RBD-positive; plus 22 iRBD patients), the authors report that two-thirds of iRBD patients had normal putaminal FDOPA scans, while RBD-positive Parkinson's disease and iRBD patients showed reduced cardiac MIBG heart:mediastinum ratios compared with RBD-negative patients. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] The aggregation review describes alpha-synuclein fibril formation as typically nucleation-dependent, with lag, elongation and maturation phases. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8347623/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] Shahnawaz and colleagues note that clinical differentiation of Parkinson’s disease and multiple system atrophy is challenging, particularly early in disease. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1984-7 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] Shahnawaz and colleagues report that their α-synuclein-PMCA assay discriminated cerebrospinal fluid samples from patients diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease from those with multiple system atrophy. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1984-7 · keywords: Alpha-synucleinopathies: PD, DLB and MSA
- [statement] NINDS describes alpha-synuclein buildup in glia as a distinguishing feature of MSA. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/multiple-system-atrophy · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] NINDS identifies tau buildup in affected brain cells as a signature of PSP. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/progressive-supranuclear-palsy · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] The MDS PSP criteria paper identifies ocular motor dysfunction, postural instability, akinesia and cognitive dysfunction as clinical predictor domains. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28467028/ · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] The Armstrong consortium criteria paper identifies corticobasal, frontal behavioral-spatial, nonfluent/agrammatic primary progressive aphasia and progressive supranuclear palsy syndromes as CBD phenotypes. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23359374/ · keywords: Atypical parkinsonism: MSA, PSP and CBD
- [statement] A Neurology study comparing the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay on CSF across 4 European laboratories, with 20 patients with DLB and 10 controls, reports average sensitivity of 78.8% (minimum 55%, maximum 100%) and average specificity of 77.5% (minimum 60%, maximum 100%). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-28) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214614 · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The diagnostic-criteria review uses DLB for dementia before or concurrently with parkinsonism and PDD for dementia in well-established Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6987529/ · keywords: Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation distinguishes parkinsonism, a set of movement symptoms, from a specific diagnosis; the MDS criteria separately assess whether Parkinson’s disease is its cause. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/understanding-parkinsons/what-is-parkinsons/types-parkinsonisms · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] For determining Parkinson’s disease as the cause of parkinsonism, the MDS criteria use absolute exclusions, red flags counterbalanced by supportive criteria, and supportive features. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474316/ · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] The MDS criteria distinguish clinically established Parkinson’s disease, prioritizing specificity, from probable disease, balancing sensitivity and specificity. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474316/ · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] NINDS states that no specific single test can definitively diagnose Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/parkinsons-disease · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
