- [statement] Beach and Adler report that autopsy-validated studies found misdiagnosis common in early clinically diagnosed Parkinson’s disease compared with patients followed for years. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6544441/ · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] The MDS clinical diagnostic criteria define motor parkinsonism as bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474316/ · keywords: Movement disorders and neurodegeneration landscape
- [statement] Assessment combines patient and informant history with cognitive testing. MDS Level I is abbreviated; Level II uses comprehensive testing across five cognitive domains, with two tests per domain. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8073727/ · keywords: PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- [statement] Stephenson and colleagues report that EMA issued a 2018 Qualification Opinion for DAT imaging as an enrichment biomarker in trials targeting early motor Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6700608/
- [statement] NINDS describes the PDBP Data Management Resource as containing clinical, genetic, imaging and biomarker data associated with Parkinson’s disease, Lewy Body Dementia and related disorders. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pdbp.ninds.nih.gov/
- [statement] EMA’s DAT imaging letter supports further development and validation; the Stephenson review reports a subsequent full Qualification Opinion in 2018 for DAT enrichment in Parkinson’s trials targeting early motor symptoms. (low confidence) (verified as of 2019-07-30) — https://media.c-path.org/wp-content/uploads/20240427170245/cpp_ema_letter_of_support_cpp_imaging_biomarker-1.pdf · keywords: Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies
- [statement] FDA letter DDT-BMQ-000157 supports binary assessment of alpha-synuclein seed amplification as an enrichment biomarker for patient selection in trials targeting disorders with common synuclein biology. ## Parkinson's disease frontier platforms: dopaminergic cell replacement, gene therapy, digital biomarkers and wearables, AI, the gut-brain axis with body-first versus brain-first subtypes, and precision medicine
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-frontier-platforms-cell-replacement-gene-therapy-digital-biomarkers-ai-gut-brain-axis-and-precision-medicine"></a>

- [statement] The authors of the original case-control study hypothesize that isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a prodromal phenotype for the body-first type, and a later longitudinal study states that the presence of rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) may be indicative of a body-first pattern. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/
- [statement] The commentary states that post hoc confounder analysis showed inclusion of indeterminate participants would not substantially change the study's main findings, while the exclusion of about one-quarter of the initial study population may limit the clinical applicability and generalizability of the subtyping criteria. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7821233/
- [statement] Applying a pragmatic approach based on motor asymmetry, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and orthostatic hypotension to a large cohort of persons with early PD (disease duration <5 years), the authors report that individuals classified as probable brain-first were more often tremor-dominant and showed a trend toward less constipation after adjusting for disease duration, age and sex. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13746290/
- [statement] One meta-analysis reports that differences in microbiome structure between PD and controls are small, and a later meta-analysis states that causality cannot be established from predominantly observational studies. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z
- [statement] Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation trials in Parkinson's disease report different primary-outcome results, and they differ in delivery route, comparator and primary-outcome time point: the trial at 4 hospitals in Finland (FMT or placebo via colonoscopy; primary end point at 6 months) reports that the primary outcome did not differ between the groups, whereas GUT-PARFECT (nasojejunal FMT with healthy donor stool or the participant's own stool; primary outcome at 12 months) reports that the MDS-UPDRS motor score improved by a mean of 5.8 points in the healthy donor group and by 2.7 points in the placebo group (p = 0.0235). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11287445/
- [statement] In the case-control PET study, the authors report that RBD-positive Parkinson's disease patients and iRBD patients showed reduced mean MIBG heart:mediastinum ratios and reduced colon donepezil standard uptake values compared with RBD-negative patients, and a scientific commentary in the same journal describes the reduced gut cholinergic and cardiac noradrenergic ligand binding in both groups as major support for the body-first disease subtype. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/
- [statement] In their own review, the authors who proposed the model report that molecular imaging studies were generally in agreement with the model, whereas structural imaging studies, such as MRI volumetry, showed conflicting findings. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38519273/
- [statement] In a longitudinal analysis using possible premotor RBD as the proxy for the body-first subtype, the authors report a lower MDS UPDRS-III score at baseline (p = 0.022) but a faster progression rate (p = 0.009) than in patients without possible RBD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11150376/
- [statement] Two meta-analyses of PD gut microbiome studies report depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae, and enrichment of Akkermansia. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z
- [statement] In limited phenotype-stratified subgroup analyses, the authors report that gut-first PD phenotypes showed potentially more pronounced dysbiosis patterns than brain-first phenotypes, a preliminary observation based on very few phenotype-stratified studies that requires validation in larger, prospective cohorts. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13642692/
- [statement] The GUT-PARFECT paper title describes a phase 2 trial, whereas the registry record NCT03808389 lists phase NA, with the record status verified 2023-01. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-03-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of machine learning in PD report a translation gap: one states that very few ML systems have been adopted for real-world use despite the large number of studies published every year, and a later review concludes that reported performance has advanced faster than evidence of generalizability and clinical implementation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The authors report an open-label phase I trial (NCT04802733) of bemdaneprocel, an investigational cryopreserved, off-the-shelf dopaminergic neuron progenitor cell product derived from human embryonic stem (hES) cells and grafted bilaterally into the putamen of patients with Parkinson's disease; the registry lists the same study as a Phase 1 study of a human embryonic stem cell-derived midbrain dopamine neuron cell therapy. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] In the Kyoto University Hospital phase I/II trial of seven patients who received iPS-cell-derived dopaminergic progenitors, the authors report that among six patients subjected to efficacy evaluation, four showed improvements in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale part III OFF score and five showed improvements in the ON scores. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08700-0
- [statement] In STEM-PD, a phase 1/2, open-label, multicenter trial of a cryopreserved, off-the-shelf dopaminergic progenitor product derived from human pluripotent stem cells, the authors report no serious adverse events attributed to the cell product, no graft-induced dyskinesias and no evidence of tumor formation on serial magnetic resonance imaging. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04525-0
- [statement] Sumitomo Pharma announced that, as of March 6, 2026, it obtained conditional and time-limited approval in Japan for the allogeneic iPS cell-derived dopaminergic neural progenitor cell product AMCHEPRY (INN: raguneprocel). (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-03-11) — https://www.sumitomo-pharma.com/news/20260306.html
- [statement] The FDA announcement states that Kebilidi (eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq) is an adeno-associated virus vector-based gene therapy indicated for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients with aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency, and that Kebilidi is the first FDA-approved gene therapy for treatment of AADC deficiency. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-11-14) — https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapy-treatment-aromatic-l-amino-acid-decarboxylase-deficiency · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] After LUMA, Biogen and Denali state they will discontinue further development of BIIB122 in idiopathic Parkinson's disease, while Denali continues the Phase 2a BEACON study in carriers of a pathogenic LRRK2 variant. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-22) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine, LRRK2-targeted therapies: small molecule and antisense
- [statement] pS65-Ubiquitin (pUb) is a PINK1 substrate, and a Michael J. Fox Foundation grant page says the differential effectiveness of PINK1 activator compounds will be determined by analyzing specific biomarkers. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11100876/ · keywords: Mitochondrial and mitophagy targets: PINK1, parkin, USP30
- [statement] Mission states that its MTX325-101 Phase 1b study is designed to establish clinical proof-of-mechanism using a wide range of biomarkers and imaging measures, and the registry's official title for NCT07630545 includes assessing CNS penetration, biodistribution, and biomarkers. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://missiontherapeutics.com/mission-therapeutics-doses-first-parkinsons-patient-in-phase-1b-study-of-potential-disease-modifying-treatment-mtx325/ · keywords: Mitochondrial and mitophagy targets: PINK1, parkin, USP30
- [statement] FDG-PET measures regional cerebral glucose metabolism and can support differentiating parkinsonian syndromes using disease-associated patterns; this is a different biological readout from presynaptic dopamine-terminal imaging. (medium confidence) — https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/58/12/1888 · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] PET measures depend on the tracer: fluorodopa uptake reflects tracer influx and decarboxylation in presynaptic dopamine assessment, whereas FDG-PET maps regional glucose metabolism and disease-related metabolic patterns. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ · keywords: Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- [statement] A NeuroDerm news page carries Tanabe Pharma's announcement of its decision to wind down the operations of its wholly owned subsidiary NeuroDerm Ltd., the company developing ND0612. (medium confidence) — https://www.neuroderm.com/our-company/news-and-events/tanabe-pharma-announces-wind-down-of-operations-at-its-wholly-owned-subsidiary-neuroderm-ltd/ · keywords: Levodopa and carbidopa formulations and delivery
- [statement] Brundin and Melki describe anterograde and retrograde transport of alpha-synuclein assemblies monitored in primary neurons grown in microfluidic devices. (low confidence) — https://www.jneurosci.org/content/37/41/9808 · keywords: Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- [statement] Rocha and colleagues describe direct-pathway spiny projection neurons as GABAergic neurons expressing Drd1 and projecting monosynaptically to the output nuclei GPi and SNpr. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] Rocha and colleagues describe indirect-pathway spiny projection neurons expressing Drd2 as projecting primarily to the GPe. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-07) — https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · keywords: Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- [statement] The 2019 MDS review called probiotics with prebiotic fiber efficacious and clinically useful on the basis of one trial; the 2022 meta-analysis instead concluded that evidence remained insufficient, noting few trials, heterogeneous preparations and high heterogeneity. These are attributed assessments with different evidence sets, not an unconditional endorsement of probiotics. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation describes free at-home PPMI screening for genetic factors and smell ability for people diagnosed with Parkinson’s. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/connect-ppmi-team

## Parkinson's disease research ecosystem and health systems: clinical trial design and endpoints, regulatory pathways at FDA and EMA, patient registries and research participation, global burden, cost and access to care
<a id="parkinson-s-disease-research-ecosystem-and-health-systems-trial-design-regulatory-pathways-registries-global-burden-and-care-access"></a>

- [statement] The EMA guideline describes milestone-event timing or the proportion reaching a milestone as possible primary endpoints in long-term randomised placebo-controlled disease-progression trials. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease_en.pdf-0
- [statement] WHO reports that levodopa/carbidopa is not accessible, available or affordable everywhere, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2023-08-09) — https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/parkinson-disease · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] Fothergill-Misbah and colleagues found that 81% (38/47) of countries in the WHO African Region included levodopa plus carbidopa or levodopa plus benserazide as a therapeutic alternative on national essential medicines lists, considering any formulation or strength. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-25) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12481222/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] The Middle East physician survey reported levodopa availability of 98% among its participating countries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13380763/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] Luo and colleagues report that 11.77 million people worldwide had Parkinson disease in 2021, using the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-01-10) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11757241/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] Yang and colleagues estimated the total economic burden of diagnosed Parkinson disease in the United States in 2017 at $51.9 billion. (low confidence) (verified as of 2020-07-09) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7347582/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] Fothergill-Misbah and colleagues state that inclusion of Parkinson disease medicines in national essential medicines lists provides no guarantee of immediate access. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-25) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12481222/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] WHO’s technical-brief launch news states that globally the prevalence of Parkinson disease has doubled in the past 25 years. (low confidence) (verified as of 2022-06-14) — https://www.who.int/news/item/14-06-2022-launch-of-who-s-parkinson-disease-technical-brief · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] The Lewin Group report defines PWPD/AP as people with Parkinson’s disease inclusive of atypical parkinsonism. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-17) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/sites/default/files/media/document/Economic%20Burden%20of%20Parkinson%E2%80%99s%20and%20Atypical%20Parkinsonism%20in%20the%20United%20States_0.pdf · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] The Middle East survey authors caution that their data were physician-reported perceptions rather than objective verification, with potential reporting bias and failure to capture within-country variability. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13380763/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] The nationwide Nigerian pharmacy survey found that only trihexyphenidyl tablets and biperiden injection were affordable under its study definition. (low confidence) (verified as of 2018-11-16) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6335528/ · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation states that annual costs surpassed the $79 billion previously projected for 2037, more than a decade early. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/about-us/news/economic-burden-2024-report · keywords: Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care
- [statement] Marek and colleagues describe PPMI as an observational, international study designed to establish biomarker-defined cohorts and identify Parkinson’s disease progression markers. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6292383/
- [statement] Iwaki and colleagues describe the AMP Parkinson’s Disease research platform as integrating whole-genome sequencing, RNA expression and clinical data harmonized across cohort studies; NINDS describes the Knowledge Platform as enabling sharing of validated and standardized datasets. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8453903/
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation describes PD GENEration as an international research study providing genetic testing and genetic counseling at no cost for people diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/pdgeneration
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation states that the Parkinson’s Outcomes Project, started in 2009, was one of the largest-ever clinical studies of Parkinson’s disease, with more than 13,000 participants in five countries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/parkinsons-outcomes-project
- [statement] The PPMI participant page states that academic and industry investigators can access the repository after administrative review and completion of a Data Use Agreement requiring privacy protection. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.ppmi-info.org/participants
- [statement] The PPMI participant page describes online participation, mailed screening tests and in-person enrollment as distinct participation routes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.ppmi-info.org/participants
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation describes Fox Trial Finder as a tool connecting volunteers with recruiting studies through searches based on location and health history, without requiring a login. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/trial-finder
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation says the Parkinson’s Outcomes Project, with 13,000+ participants, showed that the type and quality of care people receive has a major impact on their symptoms, mobility and long-term health. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/parkinsons-outcomes-project/findings
- [statement] Reviews report inconsistent validation practice in PD machine learning: in one sample of 113 studies only 65.5% (74/113) used a holdout test set to avoid potentially inflated accuracies and 38.9% (44/113) did not report on how or if models were tuned, and a review of machine learning within PPMI finds significant variability in the types of data, models, and validation procedures used across studies. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] Neuroimaging-focused reviews flag quality and translation concerns: the Movement Disorders review reports that only 20% of evaluated studies passed all five MQC and calls the number of studies failing to pass the MQC alarming, a brain-imaging machine learning review states that several issues must be addressed before these solutions can be safely integrated into clinical practice, and a deep learning review identifies a lack of data availability and interpretability of models. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] High reported accuracy coexists with weak evidence quality: a gait meta-analysis states that its GRADE analysis revealed low-quality evidence for precision and F1 score and very-low quality for accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity, and the biomarker review reports median best-model accuracy of 95.3% while 259 studies (98.1%) were at high overall risk of bias under its adapted PROBAST rules. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13362068/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The 95th centile of stride velocity has been approved by the EMA as a primary endpoint for assessing ambulant patients with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, a regulatory precedent in a disease other than Parkinson's disease. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-17) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12954611/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] The Mobilise-D consortium's perspective paper on regulatory qualification of wearable sensors to quantify real-world mobility performance in patients affected by Parkinson’s Disease reports that its qualification strategy and both the technical and clinical validation plans received highly supportive qualification advice from the European Medicines Agency. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7589106/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] Four reviews each point to standardization needs: a Movement Disorders systematic review of early Parkinson's disease calls for standardized study methodologies, a scoping review of prodromal Parkinson's disease says future research should prioritize standardized assessment, a real-world walking speed review says adoption requires improved standardization of devices, algorithms, and study methodologies, and a review of digital biomarkers for precision diagnosis and monitoring notes a lack of standardized data verification protocols. (high confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30056 · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] A three-round consensus study of 12 experts from the Mobilise-D consortium’s Parkinson’s Disease Working Group reached full consensus on a clinical utility framework for digital mobility outcomes with three main categories. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447593/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] In a systematic review of longitudinal studies in early Parkinson's disease, the authors report that three DHTs detected longitudinal changes when scales did not, with one study showing larger effect sizes for change over time of selected DHT features compared to rating scales. (low confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30056 · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] WATCH-PD was a 12-month, multicenter observational study in which 82 individuals with early, untreated PD and 50 age-matched controls wore research-grade sensors, a smartwatch, and a smartphone while performing standardized assessments in the clinic. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108794/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] The registry describes exPDite-2 as a Phase 3 multicenter, randomized, sham surgery-controlled, double-blind study in approximately 102 adults with Parkinson's disease, with participants randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive bemdaneprocel or undergo sham surgery. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06944522
- [statement] The bemdaneprocel authors caution that their data need to be interpreted cautiously in view of the open-label study design, the small patient cohort, the relatively short observation period, the expected fluctuations in PD symptoms and the possibility of placebo effects; the registry lists the study as a single group with no masking. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] At 18 months post-treatment the authors report improvements from baseline in the Moderate Cohort in mean±SE MDS-UPDRS Part III OFF scores (−18.8±6.6), describe possible clinical benefit, and state that a phase 2 randomized controlled study is planned to confirm these findings. (low confidence) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000206690 · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] The registry record for the CAP-003 phase 1/2 trial of intravenous gene therapy in Parkinson's disease with a GBA1 mutation (NCT07011771) shows the status WITHDRAWN with an enrollment count of 0, and gives as the reason that a per protocol stopping rule was met for a separate trial for a different disease state and different experimental therapy that utilized a similar technology. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-22) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT07011771 · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors, GBA1, ambroxol and lysosomal-targeted therapies
- [statement] The registry record for REGENERATE-PD (NCT06285643) lists a primary outcome of change from baseline to Month 18 on PD Motor Diary (normalized Good ON time per Hauser Diary), an actual enrollment of 59, and the status ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06285643 · keywords: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
- [statement] In a preprint, the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program authors report that among 65,509 individuals with Parkinson's disease they identified 9,019 (13.8%) potentially trial-eligible genetic variant carriers, including 6,789 GBA1, 2,084 LRRK2, and 146 dual GBA1-LRRK2 carriers. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13119358/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] The sponsors state that the Phase 2b LUMA study of BIIB122 in early-stage Parkinson's disease did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints (primary endpoint: Time to Confirmed Worsening in the modified MDS-UPDRS Part II and III combined score), and a foundation news article reports that participants treated for at least 48 weeks worsened at a similar rate to placebo. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-22) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] The sponsors state that LUMA included individuals with early-stage Parkinson's disease with or without a pathogenic LRRK2 variant, and a foundation news article states that the trial largely included patients without known genetic mutations. (medium confidence) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine, LRRK2-targeted therapies: small molecule and antisense
- [statement] The registry record lists the Phase 3 LIGHTHOUSE study of BIIB122 in participants with Parkinson's disease and pathogenic LRRK2 variants as TERMINATED, with the stated reason Sponsor Decision. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-06-26) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT05418673 · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine, LRRK2-targeted therapies: small molecule and antisense
- [statement] Authors of two papers link the failure of disease-modifying trials in PD in part to heterogeneity, with one noting that negative trials treated all PD patients as a single homogenous group. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7483040/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] The authors of a PPMI-based analysis report that trial power simulations demonstrated that enrolling DM patients could reduce sample size requirements by approximately 50% using standard trial durations compared to unstratified PD cohorts. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13616926/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] Authors report that replication of published PD subtype classifications is limited: a Delphi-panel replication of eight data-driven systems found none reproducible in LABS-PD, and a separate validation study states that replication studies in independent cohorts are currently lacking. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30056038/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] In a one-year randomized trial in early PD, transdermal nicotine did not slow progression. Of 163 randomized participants, 101 contributed to the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events were important causes of dropout, and application-site skin reactions were common. The result does not support prescribing nicotine to slow established PD. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/
- [statement] Alcohol findings in Mendelian randomization studies conflict: Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues reported lower PD risk with genetically predicted alcohol intake (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.96), whereas Courage-PD found no significant association (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39–1.18) and emphasized insufficient statistical power. Neither result alone establishes a preventive drinking recommendation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8263722/
- [statement] The 2023 correction to Hong’s caffeine meta-analysis fixed citation numbers in tables and figures; the authors stated that the scientific conclusions were unaffected. It should be consulted alongside the original meta-analysis rather than described as a retraction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9919867/
- [statement] Two Mendelian randomization studies reported inverse smoking-related associations with PD, but for different exposures: Courage-PD found an association for genetic liability to smoking initiation, whereas Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues found an association for smoking continuation (current versus former smokers). These estimates do not identify nicotine as the responsible component. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/
- [statement] The 2025 nicotine meta-analysis of five randomized trials and 346 participants found no significant short- or long-term motor benefit and no significant short-term improvement in daily functioning, cognition or quality of life, with considerable between-study heterogeneity. It does not establish preventive effects before diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12384040/
- [statement] Alcohol–PD findings disagree across study designs and reference groups: NeuroEPIC4PD reported no overall baseline or lifetime alcohol association, whereas the 2026 systematic review reported inverse associations in several pooled observational comparisons and inconsistent MR evidence. Neither result establishes that starting alcohol prevents PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7496254/
- [statement] The early-PD nicotine trial randomized 163 participants, but only 101 were assessed for the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events contributed to dropout, and patch-site skin adverse effects were common. Attrition limits interpretation of the efficacy estimate. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/
- [statement] Reviews differ on disease duration and severity: a 2024 review reported higher burden with longer duration and greater severity, whereas Lesley and colleagues’ 2025 predictor review judged disease duration, stage and motor severity inconclusive. These should not be presented as universal independent predictors. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Evidence on cognition requires qualification: the scoping review described cognitive impairment as a consistent burden predictor, while the 2025 review restricted to multivariable analyses found general cognitive function did not predict burden. These differently scoped findings should remain attributed rather than collapsed into a universal cognitive-score rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] The Cochrane review summary reported seven studies and 225 participants with PD-related mild cognitive impairment or dementia: it found no evidence of global-cognition improvement, and apparent attention/verbal-memory benefits did not survive sensitivity analysis. Evidence certainty was low, so this is uncertainty about efficacy rather than proof of ineffectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33780379/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation says targeted nutrition may slow PD advancement, whereas the randomized-trial review describes efficacy evidence as inconclusive. Attribute the optimistic guidance and the evidentiary limitation explicitly; neither establishes disease modification. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/diet-nutrition
- [statement] The MED-PARK publication is a randomized trial protocol specifying 44 participants and six months of modified Mediterranean diet versus usual diet. Its planned outcomes and enrollment timeline must not be presented as efficacy results. (low confidence) — https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/15/10/e101946
- [statement] The 2018 low-fat versus ketogenic pilot randomized 47 people with PD; 44 started and 38 completed the study. The intervention lasted eight weeks. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6175383/
- [statement] The 2026 Canoro narrative review identifies augmentation bias: telemedicine arms may receive more clinical attention than controls, so improvement cannot automatically be attributed to video delivery itself. The authors regard efficiency evidence and long-term economic sustainability as unresolved. (low confidence) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00702-026-03238-5 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] In a 2025 case-control study of 490 people with PD and 140 healthy controls, digital exclusion was greater in PD, especially because of poorer digital skills; PD severity independently predicted exclusion. These observational associations identify an implementation barrier rather than proving that PD causes digital exclusion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12625107/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A nurse-managed PD clinic demonstrated a hybrid service design combining an onsite team with remote movement-disorder expertise and multidisciplinary referral. Its implementation report establishes feasibility and access experience, rather than a controlled estimate of clinical effectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26055776/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] In a randomized trial, 122 people were allocated to an 8-month specialist-team model or general-neurologist care; 100 completed follow-up. The team group improved on PDQ-39 and motor scores, but the authors cautioned that design limitations restricted interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Randomized PD telemedicine studies support reduced travel burden and convenient specialist follow-up; these access benefits should be evaluated separately from changes in clinical outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Neither the national add-on virtual-visit trial nor the VA follow-up trial demonstrated superior clinical outcomes with telemedicine. In the national trial, quality of life did not significantly improve; in the VA trial, clinical outcomes and overall patient satisfaction were similar between groups. These findings do not establish universal equivalence for all patients or services. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2026 Canoro review recommends integrating televisits into validated hybrid care frameworks. This is consistent with the national trial authors proposing remote multidisciplinary services alongside clinic appointments and in-person home visits; the optimal combination remains a research question. (medium confidence) — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00702-026-03238-5 · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2026 Sun telehealth meta-analysis searched through June 21, 2024 and found heterogeneous quality-of-life results across intervention types and scales: pooled PDQ outcomes did not reach conventional statistical significance, whereas some other quality-of-life measures improved. Its broad intervention mix is not evidence that every virtual neurology visit improves quality of life. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12895161/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Published multidisciplinary-care findings differ by intervention and comparator: the van der Marck specialist-team trial was positive, whereas the Seid rehabilitation meta-analysis was null for quality of life; these are attributed findings from different care models, not a single universal treatment effect. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Team-based PD care brings together different experts according to individual symptoms; integration can connect a specialist, a PD nurse, and a community neurologist through an individualized treatment plan. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] In the open-label randomized trial, an individualized plan and additional home visits coordinated by specialist, nurse, and community neurologist improved reported quality of life and motor/nonmotor symptoms over six months; durability and cost-benefit remained unanswered. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29392459/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Telemedicine delivery and multidisciplinary clinical content should be distinguished: the national trial delivered neurologist visits, whereas the hybrid trial added a multidisciplinary team to office care. Their different outcomes should not be pooled as though they tested the same service. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2020 randomized trial enrolled 210 people with PD or related disorders with moderate-to-high palliative needs; at 6 months the palliative-care group had better quality of life (treatment effect 1.87; 95% CI 0.47–3.27). Its mixed diagnostic population and selected needs limit extrapolation to all PD patients. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] Benefits in one palliative-care trial should not be generalized to every ACP intervention: the 2020 intervention improved advance-directive completion, whereas PD_Pal in 2026 did not improve its primary documentation endpoint. They tested different interventions and populations. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] The buntanetap Phase 3 study in early PD did not meet its primary endpoint of MDS-UPDRS Part II, according to the published paper and Alzforum. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s44400-026-00148-x · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- [statement] The original primary endpoint of the buntanetap early-PD study was the sum of MDS-UPDRS Part II and Part III; the paper and the sponsor release state it was changed to MDS-UPDRS Part II per FDA guidance or feedback. (high confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s44400-026-00148-x · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- [statement] In its press release the sponsor reported statistical improvement in MDS-UPDRS Part II, Part III, Part II+III and Total scores in Parkinson’s patients with a >3-year diagnosis; Fierce Biotech reports this subgroup as 158 participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477845/000110465924077093/tm2418712d1_ex99-1.htm · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- [statement] In the phase 1b study of anle138b in PD (NCT04685265), the conference abstract reports 70 participants were enrolled in cohorts A-E and that anle138b was safe and well tolerated when administered 7-28 days; the registry lists 70 actual participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.mdsabstracts.org/abstract/anle138b-p1-02-a-randomised-double-blinded-placebo-controlled-phase-1b-study-to-investigate-safety-tolerability-pharmacokinetics-and-pharmacodynamics-of-the-oligomer-modulator-anle138b-in-parkins/ · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- [statement] The buntanetap Phase 3 study in early PD (registry NCT05357989) enrolled 523 participants in a 6-month, randomized, double-blind, dose-ranging design testing 10 mg and 20 mg buntanetap against placebo. (high confidence) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT05357989 · keywords: Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap

- [statement] Review authors state quality limits on the dance literature: an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews rated the overall confidence in the results of 38 reviews (69%) as critically low; a systematic review of 20 RCTs (N = 723) reported that small samples and methodological limitations resulted in low-certainty evidence across outcomes; and a systematic review of sixteen RCTs noted that performance bias cannot be controlled because participants and personnel cannot be blinded to a dance intervention and that less than half of the studies used a low-risk randomization procedure. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] Reviews state limits in trial quality: the Cochrane physiotherapy review considered the trials to be at a mixed risk of bias and said the quality of most included trials was not high; the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that methodological quality and reporting was highly variable and often inadequate and that most trials had relatively small sample sizes; and the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported that confidence in the effects ranged from moderate to very low, that studies were very small, and that larger, well-conducted studies are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] The PD COMM authors report that the trial could not be blinded, that outcomes were questionnaires completed by participants or carers (with possible performance bias), and that recruitment closed at 388 of 546 planned participants (71% of target) after the covid-19 pandemic; the NIHR report likewise states that recruitment did not meet the pre-specified power, and Parkinson's UK commented that the findings may be less clear-cut than they first appear because NHS speech and language therapy varies widely and there is no consensus on what 'standard' therapy is. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] Authors of RAS and music-based meta-analyses in Parkinson's disease state evidence-quality limits themselves: Ye and colleagues note that only two included studies had more than 100 subjects and thirteen had fewer than 50; Wang and colleagues report that lack of blinding of participants and trainers was the most common risk of bias, with twelve studies at high risk for this reason, and that the largest included study had 90 participants; Lee and Ko state that allocation concealment and blinding were not possible in most trials because of the nature of the music-related activities; and Li and colleagues rated the overall methodological quality of the included RCTs as moderate. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] In the NINDS NET-PD program, a randomized phase II futility trial of creatine and minocycline (Neurology 2006) found that neither could be rejected as futile and recommended considering both for definitive phase III trials, whereas the later Long-term Study 1 of creatine monohydrate 10 g/d (JAMA 2015; 1741 participants) was terminated early for futility at a planned interim analysis (n = 955) and concluded that creatine did not improve clinical outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16481597/
- [statement] Two coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) trials in early Parkinson disease reported conflicting results: an eighty-subject dosage-ranging trial (Arch Neurol 2002) reported less functional decline at 1200 mg/d than with placebo (P =.04) and concluded that CoQ10 appears to slow deterioration pending confirmation in a larger study, while the phase III QE3 trial (600 participants; JAMA Neurol 2014) was terminated after a prespecified futility criterion was reached and showed no evidence of clinical benefit; a 2026 review suggests the discrepancies might stem from different sample sizes and study durations. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/
- [statement] Two published meta-analyses of randomized trials of coenzyme Q10 in Parkinson disease reported no significant benefit over placebo: a 2016 analysis of five RCTs (981 patients) found that the overall effect did not favor either group for total UPDRS, and a 2017 analysis of eight studies (899 patients) found a pooled WMD of 1.02 for UPDRS part 3 (p = 0.54) and stated that routine CoQ10 treatment of PD could not be recommended. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26553164/
- [statement] Durability and generalizability remain uncertain: the pallidotomy trial called for longer and larger studies, and the systematic review recommends follow-up beyond one year with larger samples and controlled, blinded designs. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36812432/ · keywords: Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and pallidotomy
- [statement] Exact skull-density eligibility must be taken from the relevant labeling: the June 2018 tremor-dominant Parkinson’s prescriber document lists 0.45 (±0.05) or less, whereas the July 2025 S037 document lists less than 0.40. These target- and revision-specific documents should not be collapsed into one universal cutoff. - [statement] In a study of the MDS-UPDRS Motor Examination (Part III) with 728 paired investigations of 260 patients, minimal clinically important difference estimates were asymmetric: −3.25 points for minimal clinically pertinent improvement and +4.63 for worsening, using clinician global-impression anchors and distribution methods. - [statement] A critical review concluded that epidemiology alone makes causal attribution difficult because relevant exposures may precede manifest PD by decades; complementary experimental evidence increases causal plausibility. - [statement] The paraquat evidence has conflicting interpretations: Tanner and colleagues’ 2011 Agricultural Health Study nested case-control analysis reported an association with PD (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7); EPA’s page updated November 3, 2026 states that it has not found a clear link between labeled paraquat uses and PD. The regulatory statement is qualified by labeled-use conditions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-03) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/
- [statement] A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis (databases searched up to May 2019) found, across nine case-control studies, that PD occurrence was 25% higher in participants exposed to paraquat, while the only cohort investigation included showed a non-significant OR of 1.08; the authors concluded that the data indicate a positive association but that the weight-of-evidence does not enable one to assume an indisputable cause-effect relationship. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31476981/
- [statement] Tanner et al. reported an association between paraquat use and PD in FAME (110 cases, 358 controls; OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7), whereas the later AHS prospective analysis reported no statistically clear association (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.84–1.41). These overlapping study populations and different designs should not be counted as independent replications. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/
- [statement] Air-pollution findings differ across settings: a Taiwan nationwide study reported positive associations for several pollutants that persisted in multipollutant models, while a Northern Ireland study found no overall association for medium-term PM₂.₅ or NO2 exposure and medication-defined PD onset; its under-50 subgroup showed a PM₂.₅ association. These exposure windows and outcome definitions limit direct comparison. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12322442/
- [statement] The same Global Burden of Disease analysis reported male-to-female ratios of age-standardised prevalence rates of 1·40 (95% UI 1·36-1·43) in 2016 and 1·37 (1·34-1·40) in 1990, and estimated 211 296 deaths (95% UI 167 771-265 160) due to Parkinson's disease in 2016. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30287051/
- [statement] The Global Burden of Disease investigators concluded that the global burden of Parkinson's disease more than doubled over the past generation as a result of increasing numbers of older people, with potential contributions from longer disease duration and environmental factors. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30287051/
- [statement] A 2023 narrative review in J Parkinsons Dis (Dorsey and colleagues) reports that trichloroethylene (TCE) was first linked to parkinsonism in 1969, that four case studies involving eight individuals have linked occupational exposure to TCE to PD, and that a small epidemiological study associated occupational or hobby exposure with a 500% increased risk; the authors postulate that TCE contributes to the global rise of PD and state that further research is necessary to examine this hypothesis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10041423/
- [statement] The critical review by Atterling Brolin and colleagues argues that converging epidemiological and experimental evidence supports stronger environmental policy action; this is the review authors’ assessment of causality and prevention, rather than proof that every exposure causes PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11832802/
- [statement] A UK paraquat-manufacturing workforce mortality study found no evidence of increased PD mortality (SMR 0.67, 95% CI 0.18–1.72). - [statement] In the Global Burden of Disease analysis, 6·1 million (95% uncertainty interval 5·0-7·3) individuals had Parkinson's disease globally in 2016, compared with 2·5 million (2·0-3·0) in 1990; age-standardised prevalence rates increased by 21·7% (95% UI 18·1-25·3) over the same period. Improvement in overall sleep quality must not be substituted for proof of a specific sleep-disorder benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13612690/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The 2025 systematic review pooled pharmacological trials and reported improvements in insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness but no statistically significant pooled RBD benefit; certainty ranged from very low to moderate. This class-level pooling does not establish efficacy of every included drug. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706981/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The EJS ACT-PD registry specifies the equally weighted combined MDS-UPDRS Parts I and II as its primary outcome measuring progression between active-treatment and placebo arms. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-10-03) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT07207057
- [statement] After reviewing wash-in, wash-out, delayed-start and other designs in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, McGhee and colleagues favour long-term follow-up examining sustained divergence between treatment arms. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4910262/
- [statement] Mahlknecht and colleagues explain that phenoconversion endpoint events can be increased by selecting higher-risk prodromal participants, extending follow-up, or increasing sample size. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8859908/
- [statement] EMA’s questions-and-answers document on inclusion criteria states that the guideline’s definitions of de novo, early and advanced Parkinson’s disease are working definitions based on clinical practice and not intended to define exact and mutually exclusive patient populations. ## Shared
<a id="shared"></a>

- [statement] External validation is uncommon in the reviewed literature: the neuroimaging review reports that very few studies employed external test sets (8%), where accuracy was significantly lower, and the later biomarker review reports that only 20 (7.6%) of the studies met its external-validation definition and that in ten within-study comparisons external performance fell in eight. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/ · keywords: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
- [statement] The registry record for WATCH-PD, NCT03681015, lists the overall status as COMPLETED, with a status verified date of 2022-09. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-01) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT03681015 · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] In a systematic review of real-world walking speed across conditions, the authors report that no device or outcome measure that assesses walking speed in real-world conditions has been fully validated by the FDA, and that they found four letters of intent on the FDA website related to this concept. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12954611/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] In the consensus study, the authors report that the main challenge to address is the definition of clear reference value for DMOs interpretability. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447593/ · keywords: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
- [statement] The authors report that secondary and exploratory clinical outcomes showed improvement or stability, including improvement in the MDS-UPDRS Part III OFF scores by an average of 23 points in the high-dose cohort, in this open-label early-phase trial. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] The authors report that the phase I trial of bemdaneprocel achieved its primary objectives of safety and tolerability one year after transplantation, with no adverse events related to the cell product; an abstract authored by sponsor employees describes the early-phase study as having demonstrated bemdaneprocel was generally safe and well tolerated. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] The Kyoto authors state that, as an open-label trial without a control group, the influence of the placebo effect and observer bias must be considered, and that the findings of this single-centre, small-sample trial should be confirmed in multi-centre, large-sample trials with appropriate controls. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08700-0
- [statement] In STEM-PD, seven participants completed 12-month follow-up and one participant died from a pulmonary infection, and the authors state that risks were primarily associated with the immunosuppression regimen. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04525-0
- [statement] The registry record lists exPDite-2 as RECRUITING with an estimated primary completion date of 2028-10, and the sponsor-authored abstract states that the first participant was randomized and underwent surgery in August 2025. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06944522
- [statement] In a PPMI analysis, the authors report that the diffuse malignant (DM) subtype had the highest GBA1 frequency, 14.0% versus 5.9% in the mild-motor predominant (MMP) subtype. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13116718/ · keywords: PD subtypes and precision medicine
- [statement] The telephone CBT trial excluded possible dementia or marked cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score <21), active suicidal plans or intent, unstable serious illness, and primary psychotic, bipolar, or substance-use disorder; its results therefore do not establish efficacy for these excluded groups. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In a 136-person trial, eight weeks of computerized cognitive training did not improve the primary planning-accuracy outcome or subjective cognitive complaints compared with an active control. A secondary processing-speed improvement had limited clinical impact, and no group differences remained at six months. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The 2025 CBT meta-analysis included 16 RCTs and 682 participants, with searches updated through February 29, 2024; it found pooled improvements in depression and anxiety but no statistically significant pooled quality-of-life improvement. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447579/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Apparent treatment benefits need interpretation against control design and outcome choice: the telephone CBT investigators could not fully separate psychotherapy-specific effects from contact and attention, and the computerized cognitive-training investigators found only minor secondary gains with limited clinical impact despite a null primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The Fox study cannot establish causation or longitudinal slowing of PD: progression was estimated from current symptoms and diagnosis date, and the authors explicitly acknowledged the cross-sectional limitation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/
- [statement] The MIND/Mediterranean symptom analysis cannot establish causality: its authors describe a cross-sectional method, lack of temporal analysis, a largely white and wealthy US sample, possible co-occurring protective behaviors and unvalidated brief questionnaire scales. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/
- [statement] The MIND/Mediterranean observational association has limited generalizability: the Fox cohort was predominantly white, wealthy and US-based, and healthier co-occurring behaviors or access could confound the association. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/
- [statement] Orthostatic-hypotension assessment includes blood-pressure measurements supine and after three minutes standing, plus assessment of possible causes such as hypovolemia or blood-pressure-lowering drugs. This is relevant when falls are unexplained or accompanied by standing-related symptoms. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Cochrane review found a smaller probable reduction in the number of people experiencing at least one fall (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.80–1.00), while effects on fall-related fractures and adverse events remained uncertain. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9169540/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Bathroom safety guidance recommends properly anchored grab bars, seated bathing options, better lighting and clear routes. Towel racks and similar fixtures should not be used as grab bars. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] A walking aid does not necessarily reduce freezing. A small comparative study found that both standard and wheeled walkers slowed walking, the standard walker increased freezing and a laser attachment added no benefit; a systematic review likewise found limited and heterogeneous evidence for mobility aids. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14499200/ · keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Travel guidance recommends carrying extra medication and keeping medication in carry-on luggage rather than depending on checked bags. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/traveling · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] Driving fitness assessment should consider motor function, cognition, vision, sleepiness and medication effects; specialist on-road and off-road assessment can help resolve concerns. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10928339/ · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] Travel planning guidance recommends allowing extra time, scheduling rest around arrival, and avoiding an overloaded itinerary. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/traveling · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] Suggested workplace adaptations include scheduling difficult tasks during better-functioning periods, breaks, ergonomic or computer adaptations, and exploring flexible hours or telecommuting where feasible. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/library/fact-sheets/employment · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] A 2018 driving meta-analysis found poorer on-road and simulator outcomes in PD, but no significant difference in self-reported real-life crash involvement; its authors cautioned against PD-specific relicensure mandates based on self-reported crash data alone. (low confidence) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000006132 · keywords: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] The national virtual-visit trial used a motor assessment that excluded rigidity and balance; the authors also identified difficulties assessing gait because of technology, camera view, and the absence of trained clinicians. Remote follow-up therefore leaves examination gaps. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2017 national trial randomized 195 people and added 4 virtual specialist visits over 1 year to usual care. It reported 98% completing at least one virtual visit, 91% of scheduled virtual visits completed, and median savings of 88 minutes and 38 miles per visit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The 2020 integrated-care review found only a small quality-of-life benefit in its outpatient subgroup; substantial overall heterogeneity and risk of bias limit generalization to all multidisciplinary models. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32598094/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A nonrandomized trial found only small initial benefits from expert assessment and regional allied-health referrals; benefits disappeared after adjustment for baseline disease severity. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23988337/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] The national virtual-visit trial predominantly enrolled white, college-educated participants already familiar with the internet and frequently already receiving specialist care; its authors cautioned that results might not generalize to the broader PD population. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] That national trial did not demonstrate improved quality of life from adding virtual visits to usual care, while saving a median 88 minutes and 38 miles per visit. A nonsignificant difference does not itself establish equivalence or noninferiority. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Advance care planning includes clarifying values, choosing a surrogate, discussing future medical care and documenting preferences; paperwork is one part of the process. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6556088/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] Advance care planning is a continuing discussion of future care needs, wishes and preferences, including decisions for a time when a person may be unable to decide independently. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8355553/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] Individual readiness and timing matter: interview findings support regularly revisiting information preferences, while the PD_Pal contextual analysis found both resistance when discussion felt premature and cognitive limitations that could obstruct later participation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8355553/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] PD_Pal’s authors identify fragmented electronic-record documentation and limited visibility as possible reasons recorded preferences may be missed; documentation alone may not capture the quality or process of ACP discussions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771020/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] The 2020 trial found improved advance-directive completion among secondary outcomes, but its lack of demographic diversity and conduct at experienced academic centers limit generalizability. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] Lum and colleagues recommend starting ACP discussions early because later communication and cognitive difficulties can reduce participation; they also recommend checking readiness, knowledge and information needs rather than assuming everyone wants the same discussion. - [statement] In that 2020 trial, among participants without an advance directive at baseline, six-month completion was 53% with palliative care versus 26% with standard care; the health-care-proxy completion comparison was not significant. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] In the 2021 qualitative interview study of 20 patients, most wanted ACP discussion with a clinician and the majority preferred clinician initiation early in the disease; preferred information timing varied. - [statement] Trial reports and reviews state that acupuncturists cannot be blinded and that the evidence base is geographically concentrated: Yan et al. note the nature of acupuncture resulted in the acupuncturists being unblinded; Cui et al. state that acupuncturists could not be blinded, that the evidence base is small and predominantly from China, and that the predominance of positive findings raises the possibility that effects may be overestimated if negative or null trials remain unpublished; and Yu et al. state that full double-blinding was rarely feasible and allocation concealment was often inadequately reported. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether high-intensity aerobic exercise gives greater motor benefit than moderate intensity: the SPARX phase 2 trial found that only its high-intensity treadmill arm reached a predefined nonfutility threshold, whereas a systematic review of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise found no statistically significant differences versus moderate or low intensity and called the evidence too limited to allow recommendations for clinical practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5838616/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] The trial registry record for NCT04284436 lists SPARX3 as active, not recruiting (status verified 2026-04), with enrollment 370 (actual), primary completion estimated 2027-07-31, last update posted 2026-07-10, and no results posted. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT04284436 · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Reported effects of LSVT LOUD on speech intelligibility are mixed: RCSLT guidance (last updated December 2025) says eight studies reported improvement and two did not, depending on how intelligibility was measured; the Cochrane review comparing therapy techniques (searches up to April 2011) says all included trials assessed intelligibility and almost all results were not statistically significant; and a meta-analysis by Pu and colleagues reported pooled speech intelligibility of 16.54 (95% CI 11.35-21.72) with heterogeneity of 77%. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.rcslt.org/members/clinical-guidance/parkinsons/parkinsons-guidance/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] The PD COMM pilot trial reported a trend to improvement in the Voice Handicap Index at three months with both LSVT LOUD and standard speech and language therapy versus control, whereas the full PD COMM trial reported benefit for LSVT LOUD but no evidence of benefit for NHS speech and language therapy versus no therapy. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5763537/ · keywords: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
- [statement] A review by LSVT researchers, two of whom disclose ownership interest in LSVT Global, Inc., tabulates LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG as standardized protocols with a dosage of 4 consecutive days a week for 4 weeks (16 sessions in one month); the PD COMM trial likewise delivered LSVT LOUD as four sessions each week over four weeks. - [statement] A nine-patient double-blind randomized crossover trial using consecutive one-month treatment periods and beta-band dual-threshold control reported no statistically significant adaptive-versus-continuous DBS differences; the authors reported between-patient heterogeneity and called for adequately powered follow-up. - [statement] Conventional initial monopolar testing commonly holds pulse width at 60 μs and frequency at 130 Hz while amplitude is increased to identify benefit and side-effect thresholds. - [statement] A small retrospective psychosis cohort found no statistically significant mortality difference between pimavanserin and quetiapine; retrospective design, mixed PD/Lewy-body-dementia enrollment, concomitant treatment and limited power prevent concluding equivalent mortality safety. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7061324/
- [statement] Apathy is reduced motivation and goal-directed thinking or action; it can occur independently of depression. The 2024 German guideline stresses that distinguishing apathy from depressive affect is clinically challenging. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/
- [statement] The 2019 MDS review rated rasagiline efficacious but only possibly useful for fatigue, explicitly because the supporting positive trial was small and low quality; this is a historical rating, not proof of established long-term benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] PANDA did not meet its primary pain endpoint at week 16. The 2019 MDS review accordingly found insufficient efficacy evidence for prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone, despite a possibly useful practice rating based partly on its use for severe chronic pain outside PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26494524/ · keywords: PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- [statement] The AASM recommends a safe RBD sleeping environment: remove weapons and dangerous bedside objects, pad or move sharp furniture, place a soft surface beside the bed, and consider separate sleeping for severe uncontrolled behaviors. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071384/ · keywords: PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- [statement] The EMA guideline states that dopamine uptake or receptor-density imaging is insufficient as a surrogate because correlation with meaningful persistent clinical change has not been established. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease_en.pdf-0
- [statement] McGhee and colleagues warn that an inadequately short wash-out can leave symptomatic carry-over and falsely suggest disease modification. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4910262/
- [statement] The MDS-UPDRS Motor Examination study used anchor- and distribution-based methods in 260 patients and estimated minimal clinically important changes of -3.25 points for improvement and 4.63 points for worsening. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26578041/
- [statement] FDA states that a biomarker letter of support does not imply biomarker qualification and does not endorse a specific biomarker test or device. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.fda.gov/drugs/biomarker-qualification-program/letter-support-los · keywords: Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies
- [statement] FDA’s Vyalev approval letter states that AbbVie’s amendment dated August 16, 2024 constituted a complete response to FDA’s June 18, 2024 action letter. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-10-16) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2024/216962Orig1s000ltr.pdf · keywords: Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies
